Blackstone will provide $750 million for Phase 3 development of Ollin Biosciences’ retinal disease bispecific as Johnson & Johnson looks to bolster its eye therapeutics pipeline after several setbacks.
Johnson & Johnson is buying ophthalmology biotech Ollin Biosciences and its late-stage bispecific antibody for $2.2 billion upfront.
The acquisition will also give Ollin shareholders the chance to collect up to $1.125 billion in milestone payments, according to a Monday news release . The company announcement came swiftly on the heels of a Financial Times report Sunday evening that J&J was expected to buy the Texas biotech for up to $3.4 billion.
At the same time, J&J has also inked a funding agreement with private equity (PE) firm Blackstone Life Sciences to support the late-stage testing of Ollin’s OLN324—the bispecific at the center of Monday’s buyout. Once the acquisition closes, Blackstone will pay J&J $750 million over the course of several years to fully fund Phase 3 development, with the investor then able to receive undisclosed regulatory and sales milestone payments, plus single digit royalties.
The deal adds to Blackstone’s string of Big Pharma funding agreements. Just last week, the PE giant offered Pfizer up to $1.5 billion to support the pharma’s Metsera-acquired obesity drug berobenatide. In 2025, Blackstone signed a similar agreement with Merck to fund the development of the TROP2 antibody-drug conjugate sac-TMT.
Funding
Pfizer snags $1.5B financing from PE firm Blackstone to support Metsera asset
With 10 active or planned Phase 3 trials underway for Metsera’s berobenatide, Pfizer has signed a deal with Blackstone Life Sciences to finance the program to approval.

Read more
Ollin’s OLN324 is a next-gen antibody designed to selectively target two drivers of retinal disease—vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and angiopoietin-2 (Ang2)—to improve control of retinal fluid and potentially extend time between treatments.
The asset is being developed to treat conditions such as wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic macular edema (DME)—two serious retinal vascular diseases that can lead to vision loss. In the mid-stage trial called JADE , OLN324 demonstrated faster and greater improvements in retinal anatomy compared to Genentech’s blockbuster Vabysmo in both DME and wet AMD, as well as greater vision gains.
Ollin emerged publicly in September 2025 with $100 million and OLN324, which was discovered by Chinese partner Innovent Biologics. In June of this year, Ollin secured an eye-popping $330 million series B to advance the VEGF/Ang2 antibody. At the time, the biotech said it planned on launching Phase 3 testing by the end of the year.
For J&J, the proposed acquisition would bolster the New Jersey pharma’s leadership in ophthalmology, according to the company. Currently, the pharma doesn’t sell any retinal disease drugs but touts the contacts brand Acuvue and Tecnis intraocular lenses.
J&J has taken several hits to its retinal disease pipeline this year, handing back rights to MeiraGTx for the investigational gene therapy for X-linked retinitis pigmentosa in the spring after a Phase 3 miss. The pair linked up in 2019, with J&J paying $100 million upfront in a deal worth up to $440 million total to develop the therapy, known as bota-vec.
In April, MeiraGTx paid $25 million upfront to regain the rights to bota-vec. It is planning a regulatory run for the asset despite the late-stage fail. J&J is also eligible for an undisclosed milestone payment tied to U.S. approval and sales performance of bota-vec and could collect double-digit royalties starting in mid-2029.
Then there’s Hemera Biosciences’ AAV2-based gene therapy for geographic atrophy, which J&J axed this summer after a data review, according to Fierce Biotech . The pharma initially secured rights to the asset in a 2020 deal for which financials were not disclosed.

A planned master’s degree in mining and mineral processing would take 12 to 16 months. Credit: The Northern Miner
By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
Memorial University is developing a shorter route to training mining professionals as the industry faces a wait of almost six years for the first graduates from its proposed undergraduate mining engineering program.
A planned master’s degree in mining and mineral processing would take 12 to 16 months and help existing employees gain skills sooner, Salim Ahmed, Memorial’s head of process engineering, told The Northern Miner ’s Devan Murugan in an interview this month in St. John’s. The university also plans shorter courses for practising engineers and other workers.
“It will have flexibility to accommodate the need of the industry,” Ahmed said. “There will be significant demand for skilled manpower. At the same time, we’re not getting enough people, and people are retiring.”
The challenge extends beyond replacing retiring workers: graduates will need to handle autonomous equipment, growing volumes of operational data and new maintenance technologies. Memorial aims to integrate those skills throughout its teaching, with an undergraduate program targeting a fall 2027 intake.

Hyundai Finally Confirms Spring 2027 US Launch for the Ioniq 6 N Electric Performance Sedan
8 photos
Photo: Hyundai / edited
South Korea's largest automaker is bringing the Ioniq 6 N to America next spring. The electric performance sedan is listed by Hyundai Motor America with extremely limited availability for the 2027 model year.
Unveiled a year ago at AutoMobility LA, the Ioniq 6 N in North American spec was originally intended to hit showrooms during 2026. The company's latest model year info pushes the launch into spring 2027 without any explanation for the delay, though one has to consider that very few peeps will be willing to spend just around $60,000 for a compact-sized Hyundai sedan.
Pricing has yet to be confirmed, but we do know the Ioniq 5 N crossover retails from $59,900 before destination, taxes, and optional extras. Using this logic, the sleeker electric vehicle should cost more. Speaking of which, the Ioniq 5 N carries over unchanged for model year 2027.
Hyundai Motor America isn't bringing lesser versions of the Ioniq 6 to the United States for 2027, leaving the N as the only derivative. In a similar fashion to the 5, the 6 in N flavor uses a dual-motor setup that promises 166 kilowatts for the front drive unit and 282 kilowatts for the rear motor. That's 601 mechanical horsepower, with N Grin Boost mode unlocking a further 40 for up to 10 seconds at a time.
Maximum torque reaches 568 pound-feet (770 Newton-meters), and you need every bit of torque when you remember how heavy the Ioniq 6 N actually is. Despite packing an 84-kWh battery, the zero-emission sedan requires 3.2 seconds to hit 60 miles per hour (97 kilometers per hour).
Photo: Hyundai Its top speed is anything but interesting after Tesla cracked 200 miles per hour with the now-discontinued Model S Plaid. If you insist, Hyundai Motor America says that 159 miles per hour (256 kilometers per hour) is doable with the right tires. Thankfully, the South Korean automaker understands that performance means a lot more than merely straight-line performance.
The redesigned suspension geometry, electronically controlled dampers, performance rubber, and electronic limited-slip diff are some highlights, along with revised bushings, stronger axles, and various structural reinforcements for improved body control and steering response. Even the rear anti-roll bar is stronger. From a visual standpoint, the prominent rear wing helps the Ioniq 6 N stand out in the crowd.
A wilder-looking machine than its crossover-bodied brother, the newcomer rolls on forged wheels that wear Pirelli P Zero tires. The wheel-tire combo frames four- and single-piston calipers that squeeze on 15.7- and 14.2-inch discs, with regenerative braking capable of providing up to 0.6 Gs of deceleration in the most aggressive operating mode.
While it may feature a large battery and 800-volt goodies, the driving range is best described as abysmal for a 2027 model year electric vehicle. 245 miles (394 kilometers) is the most you can expect with a full charge, and that's awful by all accounts. Not only do you get more range from a base Chevy Equinox EV crossover, but even the Tesla Model 3 Performance offers more, specifically 316 miles (509 kilometers).
Another part certain customers may not like about the Ioniq 6 N is the N e-Shift thingy, which simulates a transmission through programmed torque adjustments and gear ratios. N Active Sound+ is a bit on the gimmicky side of electric performance driving as well, as is the ambient shift light system that uses the cabin's ambient lighting to indicate simulated shift points.

source_document.body:
I spent my early career working on space systems at Los Angeles Air Force Base: satellite technology, space defense infrastructure—the kind of work where failure isn’t an option and the mission is clear. What that experience gave me, more than anything, was a framework for thinking about critical systems: what they depend on, where they’re vulnerable, and what it actually takes to keep them running.
I think about the grid the same way. Electricity is more than an essential service. It’s the infrastructure that supports everything else: hospitals, water systems, communications networks, manufacturing facilities, and military installations. When it works, most people don’t think about it. When it doesn’t, the consequences are immediate and widespread. That’s why I view grid resilience not simply as an energy issue, but as a national resilience issue.
Today, that resilience is being tested. Utilities are confronting rising demand from data centers, electrification, new manufacturing investments, and other sources of load growth, all while managing infrastructure that was designed for a different era. New generation and transmission will be essential to meeting those needs, but many of those investments require years to permit, finance, and construct.
That reality has elevated the role of demand-side management. The industry often frames reliability and sustainability as competing priorities. In practice, demand-side resources are one of the few tools capable of advancing both. By reducing unnecessary consumption and shifting load away from periods of peak demand, they can strengthen reliability while helping utilities achieve sustainability goals more cost-effectively.
But it’s important to be clear about both what demand-side management can do and what it cannot.
Where Demand Management Genuinely Helps
The strongest case for demand-side work is speed. Large infrastructure projects, including new generation resources, transmission lines, and substation upgrades, can take a decade or more to move from planning to operation. Load growth isn’t waiting. Demand-side programs can often be designed, deployed, and producing measurable results within months rather than years. That matters when utilities are managing reliability pressures in real time.
Energy efficiency reduces the amount of electricity needed in the first place. Demand flexibility changes when electricity is used. Together, they provide utilities and grid operators with additional tools to manage peak demand, defer certain capital investments, and create breathing room while larger infrastructure projects move forward.
Demand-side resources also offer a practical bridge between reliability and sustainability objectives. Every kilowatt-hour that doesn’t need to be generated reduces pressure on the system. In many cases, efficiency improvements can help utilities accommodate growing demand while lowering costs and reducing associated emissions. Those benefits become increasingly valuable as utilities work to balance affordability, reliability, and environmental goals simultaneously.
Some utilities are already treating demand-side resources with the same seriousness as supply-side investments, incorporating energy efficiency and demand flexibility into long-term resource planning. That shift reflects a broader recognition that managing demand is no longer a supplemental strategy. In many territories, it is becoming an essential part of the reliability toolkit.
For utilities facing rising peak loads, interconnection constraints, and increasing pressure to control costs, that approach isn’t simply good policy. It’s good operations.
Where It Falls Short
Demand management is not a substitute for supply. It is a complement to it, and confusing the two creates expectations that no demand-side program can realistically meet.
Large industrial facilities, advanced manufacturing operations, and data centers require dependable, continuous power. Demand flexibility works best for loads that can be shifted or reduced during periods of system stress. It is far less effective for operations where interruptions carry significant operational or financial consequences. Utilities serving these customers still need generation and transmission capacity. Efficiency programs do not eliminate that requirement.
There is also a fairness question the industry continues to navigate. Some demand-side programs may disproportionately benefit customers who have the capital, technology, or flexibility to participate, while broader infrastructure costs remain shared across the entire customer base. Utilities and regulators will need to continue refining program design to ensure benefits are accessible and equitable.
Measurement presents another challenge. Demonstrating that energy savings are real, additional, and persistent requires rigorous evaluation. Reliable outcomes depend on reliable measurement, and not every program is designed with the same level of discipline and accountability.
Scale is a limiting factor as well. Demand-side resources can meaningfully reduce growth in electricity consumption and help manage system peaks, but they are unlikely to offset the full magnitude of anticipated load growth on their own. They narrow the gap. They do not close it.
Any honest discussion about grid reliability should begin with that recognition.
What Utilities Are Actually Contending With
The utilities I speak with are not debating whether demand-side resources have value. They do. The challenge is determining how to integrate those resources into planning frameworks that were built for slower demand growth, more predictable consumption patterns, and a clearer separation between the supply side and the demand side of the equation.
That integration requires more than good intentions. It requires data, customer engagement, program infrastructure, and regulatory frameworks that allow demand-side investments to be evaluated alongside supply-side alternatives. In many jurisdictions, those frameworks are still evolving.
Utilities are also grappling with questions of cost allocation, resource adequacy, and long-term planning amid unprecedented uncertainty. The assumptions that guided resource planning for decades are changing. Load forecasts are becoming more dynamic. Customer expectations are rising. The need for flexibility is growing.
Against that backdrop, the most effective strategies are not built around a single solution. They combine new generation, upgraded transmission, demand-side resources, and regulatory structures that support integrated planning. Utilities that are succeeding in this environment are treating demand-side management as a core component of their strategy while remaining realistic about its limitations.
The industry does not have the luxury of choosing between reliability and sustainability. It must deliver both.
Demand-side management will not solve every challenge facing the grid. It cannot replace the need for new generation, upgraded transmission, or continued infrastructure investment. But it can reduce consumption, ease pressure during peak periods, lower emissions, and buy time while larger investments come online. For utilities managing real reliability pressure right now, that’s not a small thing.
The grid is a critical system. Treat it like one, and use every tool available to keep it running.
— Rich McBee is president and CEO of CLEAResult , North America’s largest provider of energy efficiency, energy transition, and energy sustainability services.

Tesla is going to build the Cybercab in Germany. The company confirmed today a first €3 billion investment in a new production building at Giga Berlin designed for up to 1 million Cybercabs a year, with production planned for 2029.
That’s a lot of robotaxis for a continent where Tesla can’t operate a single one. Under current EU rules, a driverless vehicle model is capped at 1,500 registrations a year.
Tesla’s 2029 Cybercab plan for Grünheide
Plant manager André Thierig announced the decision on X after Tesla told employees on Monday:
If you ever wondered, what we would be doing at Giga Berlin with all the land that we have… We are expanding! Cybercab production is coming to Giga Berlin! Today we announced a first investment of around € 3b in a new manufacturing building with an anticpated start of… pic.twitter.com/vpcDdxoqlW — André Thierig (@AndrThie) November 16, 2026
Per Tesla’s statement, the €3 billion pays for the new production hall north of the existing plant, plus ancillary buildings and a second wastewater treatment plant. Tesla plans to file the building application before the end of the year, break ground in the first half of 2027, and start production in 2029. The company says it will be “the technologically most advanced Tesla factory in the world.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
It leaked a few hours earlier. Steven Scholtysek, an automation engineer at the plant, posted that Elon Musk personally signed off on the project last week and that the new hall will be bigger than the original factory.
The building isn’t new. Tesla laid out a plan to take Giga Berlin to 1 million vehicles a year in its 2023 permit filings and has been clearing land for it since. What’s new is the product. Until today, Tesla had only said the second hall wouldn’t be another Model Y factory.
A plant that never hit its first target
Giga Berlin still builds only the Model Y. Tesla has been hiring again at Giga Berlin this year as European demand came back , with a goal of 7,500 cars a week. Even at that pace, the plant would fall short of the 500,000 units a year Tesla promised when it opened in 2022.
Tesla is also adding 4680 battery cell production at the site , with 18 GWh of annual capacity planned.
So the new hall alone is rated for twice what the entire existing plant was supposed to build. And it comes after Musk tied the Berlin expansion to the plant’s works council election in March, warning workers against IG Metall’s influence.
The EU problem
The EU has a type-approval path for fully driverless vehicles, but it’s a “small series” scheme limited to 1,500 registrations per vehicle type per year across the whole EU. In March, the Commission lifted that cap for automated valet parking. Robotaxis are still stuck in the small-series track.
Tesla also has no approval anywhere in Europe for its software to drive without supervision. The Dutch RDW approved the supervised version, now called Tesla Assisted Driving, and nine other countries recognize that approval. It still requires a driver paying attention. The Cybercab has no steering wheel.
Rules can move in three years. The Commission has said it wants large-series approval for other driverless uses, and a UN regulation for automated driving systems is in the works. But as of today, Tesla is committing €3 billion to a vehicle it can’t sell in volume in Europe.
Tesla could export from Berlin, of course. But 1 million Cybercabs a year on top of Giga Texas implies a robotaxi business many times bigger than anything on the road today. Texas, where Cybercab production started in April , had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October. And Tesla just opened personal Cybercab orders at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 monthly subscription , usable only inside its Robotaxi geofences.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla can’t even launch its driver-assist system in Europe under its own name. What it’s rolling out there isn’t “Full Self-Driving.” It’s “Tesla Assisted Driving,” a level 2 system that needs a driver watching the road at all times, and it took a long fight with regulators to get it approved in 10 countries.
The Cybercab is a much harder sell. No steering wheel, no pedals, so it has to be certified as a level 4 vehicle with nobody inside to take over. That’s a completely different approval from anything Tesla has gotten in Europe. As of this spring, the EU said no automaker had even used its existing driverless approval path.
And the US program doesn’t inspire confidence. Robotaxi is still confined to geofences, still off highways, and it keeps crashing: Tesla had reported 22 incidents to NHTSA by July, and our analysis of the data earlier this year put it at one crash every 57,000 miles, roughly 9 times worse than the average human driver, with a safety monitor on board. The only reason those crashes don’t get more attention is that they happen at low speed. Of course they do. Tesla keeps the cars on slow city streets. Put the same system on the autobahn and we’d expect more crashes, and worse ones.

That’s the kind of news you have to want to believe. Tesla’s driver-assistance efforts are actually running into serious trouble in Europe. They still haven’t received approval for Level 2++ in Germany, while Mercedes, for example, already has it. They’ve also been told they can no longer use the term FSD because it’s considered misleading advertising. More importantly, Tesla isn’t conducting any Level 4 testing here, and that’s going to be a prerequisite for getting approvals in Europe. You can’t just self-certify your system in this field over here. So this is pretty typical Tesla news. A lot of hype, but absolutely nothing behind it.

This is Musk’s modus operandi for the last few years: bet on autonomy before it’s ready. Tesla removed the Cybercab’s steering wheel assuming the software would be solved by the time it mattered. It wasn’t, and now Tesla is putting €3 billion into a German factory on the same assumption.
Good for the workers in Grünheide, and maybe the hall can build something else if this doesn’t work out. But spending €3 billion to build up to 1 million steering-wheel-less cars a year for a market where Tesla can’t legally run a single one, based on a program that hasn’t left the geofence in Texas, is extremely risky.
Will there be one unsupervised Cybercab carrying paying passengers in Europe when the Grünheide line starts in 2029? We wouldn’t bet on it.

Suzuki Recalls Toyota RAV4 PHEV-Twinned 2026 Across Over Hybrid Control Software Issue
7 photos
Photo: Suzuki
Previously used to designate a 250-cc motorcycle, the Across nameplate returned in 2020 for a plug-in hybrid crossover that isn't actually produced by Suzuki. Essentially a rebadged Toyota RAV4 PHEV with minor stylistic changes, the Across has been recalled for motor-generator control electronics that may fail to initialize as intended.
A failed initialization forces the compact-sized model into limp mode, and in certain cases, it may also cut electric propulsion altogether at high speeds. Toyota has already launched a substantially larger safety recall for the RAV4 PHEV in the United States market, where documents published by the NHTSA offer a lot more detail than Germany's KBA does.
Per the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt, which is Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority, an estimated 1,218 vehicles have to be updated across Europe. The Japanese automaker moved 199 such vehicles in Germany alone. Referred to as 99XW by Suzuki, the campaign covers 2026 model year Across crossovers produced between March 30, 2026 and September 2, 2026.
Just like the RAV4 with plug-in hybrid assistance, the PHEV-only Across relies on a 2.5-liter naturally aspirated inline-four developed and produced by Toyota. Together with the plug-in side of the powertrain, the system generates in excess of 300 horsepower at full chatter. Its high-voltage battery, meanwhile, is rated at 22.7 kilowatt-hours.
Instead of mechanical all-wheel drive, the Across further uses the e-rear axle of the RAV4 PHEV. The larger of the two Japanese automakers calls it Electronic On-Demand AWD because the rear-mounted electric drive unit does not operate at all times. Instead, the motor in question supplies instant torque when the vehicle detects a loss of traction at the front or during hard acceleration.
Photo: Suzuki Most of the time, the RAV4 PHEV and the Across operate in FWD mode to save fuel. In Europe, the Across is exclusively offered with electrified all-wheel drive for 2026. As of this writing, the Across is the most expensive Suzuki automobile in Germany. Slotted well above the e Vitara and the internal combustion Vitara, the Across is advertised from 55,490 euros at the very least.
A 4,500-euro electrified vehicle subsidy is advertised as well, along with four paint colors, and a weighted combined energy consumption of 13.0 kWh/100 km plus 1.4 liters of dinosaur juice per 100 kilometers. Without any juice in the high-voltage battery, the combined fuel consumption is 5.4 l/100 km (43.6 mpg US).
Given the complexity of the Across' powertrain, the combustion engine and the electric motors have to coordinate their output as the vehicle moves between different operating conditions. The control system, therefore, must initialize the motor-generator units correctly. G92A0-42460 is the part number of the motor-generator electronic control unit.
Integrated into the inverter assembly, this ECU manages the electric motor-generator units. Toyota became aware of this problem when a Japanese-market RAV4 PHEV displayed warning lights and subsequently reverted to front-wheel-drive operation in limp mode.
For 2026 Suzuki Across owners, authorized service centers must reprogram the motor-generator control unit. Of course, at no charge whatsoever.
Via // KBA

context_references.quote: Lori’s Designer Shoes dropped its flat $10 fee on orders under $150 and switched to calculated shipping, footwear buyer Matt Andre said in the same report.

source_document.body:
Small online sellers are raising free-shipping minimums, charging for returns and absorbing higher label costs as the U.S. Postal Service moves to make its fuel surcharge permanent. USPS filed notice Nov. 12 to convert the 8% charge it added to package prices in April into an 11% fuel surcharge on Jan. 17 , according to its price announcement . The same day, prices for Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select would rise an average of 5.9%. The Postal Regulatory Commission will review the changes before they take effect.
The higher fuel surcharges come against a backdrop of higher shipping rates despite consumers’ demand for free shipping. Some sellers have already adjusted their free shipping policies. TickWise 3 Moms Organics, an Indiana maker of natural insect repellent, raised its free-shipping minimum to $100 from $75, founder Lisa-Jae Eggert told Modern Retail in June for its report on brands rewriting shipping policies as fuel costs rise . Her cost to ship a package has climbed to about $8.42 from $5.36, she said.
“Raising those minimum thresholds for free shipping is a necessity,” Eggert said. “It’s not something I want to do.”
The increases land as the Q4 2026 TD Cowen/AFS Freight Index projects ground parcel rates per package will reach a record 43.3% above the index’s January 2018 baseline . The index also found UPS’s increases concentrated among small and midsize customers, FreightWaves’ Eric Kulisch noted as parcel costs neared a record . This comes even as UPS courts small businesses with new digital tools . UPS raises rates an average of 5.9% on Dec. 21 and FedEx follows on Jan. 4, according to Transportation Insight .
Higher minimums carry their own risk
Joe & Bella, which sells adaptive clothing, tested the same move, raising its minimum to $100 from $75. Conversion dropped by more than half, so the company reverted, Modern Retail reported.
“Our site conversion absolutely tanked,” co-founder and CEO Jimmy Zollo told Modern Retail.
Other retailers are changing what shoppers see at checkout. Lori’s Designer Shoes dropped its flat $10 fee on orders under $150 and switched to calculated shipping, footwear buyer Matt Andre said in the same report. Todd Shelton now subtracts return shipping from customers’ refunds, a first for his 23-year-old men’s clothing company in New Jersey, CNBC reported in its look at small retailers bracing for holiday shipping costs .
Makers absorb the label cost
Makers who buy labels one at a time have less room to move. When Jenni Shields opened Evie Pearl Handmade, her hair accessories shop, eight years ago, a label cost her $2.93, she told CNBC. Her average label ran about $4.50 last year and nearly $6 at the post office counter in October. She charges customers $6 for shipping, about $1.50 of it for packaging.
“I am losing money at this point, and I’ve really taken a huge hit this year,” Shields told CNBC. “I can’t compete with Amazon on the free shipping. I can’t do that. I can’t afford that.”
Marketplace sellers are making the same point on X. Replying to an Oct. 23 post about eBay’s USPS label changes, the account Rip and Ship Report wrote, “label goes up, margin shrinks, and you never touched a thing.”
For some sellers, postage is one line in a longer list of costs. Jeffrey Hitte posted on X on Nov. 12 that he had closed his Etsy shop, citing its listing, renewal, transaction and processing fees and ad fees he said he could not opt out of. Etsy charges a 6.5% transaction fee on the item price plus shipping, according to its fee policy . Shops under $10,000 in annual sales can opt out of its 15% Offsite Ads fee , while larger shops must participate at 12%.
“You stopped being a marketplace for makers and became a toll booth. Goodbye,” Hitte wrote.
USPS adds its first fuel fee
FedEx and UPS have charged fuel surcharges for years and have reset their tables to keep those fees elevated even when diesel falls. USPS had not. The agency proposed the 8% charge in March as fuel prices climbed, and it took effect April 26 on Priority Mail, Priority Mail Express, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select.
“We have steadfastly avoided surcharges and this charge is less than one-third of what our competitors charge for fuel alone,” the Postal Service said in its March 25 announcement .
USPS then layered holiday prices on top from Oct. 4 through Jan. 17. A retail Ground Advantage package of up to 3 pounds costs 50 cents more in Zones 1 through 4 and 75 cents more in Zones 5 through 9, according to the agency’s holiday price notice .
The holiday prices end Jan. 17, when the 11% surcharge replaces the 8% charge. USPS said it will reevaluate the surcharge in July 2027 based on fuel prices in the first half of the year.
Small businesses raise prices as costs climb
A net 33% of small-business owners raised average selling prices in October, and a net 37% plan increases in the next three months, the highest reading since July 2022, according to the NFIB Small Business Economic Trends report for October . The survey does not ask about shipping, but owners’ written comments in the report do.
“Shipping costs are a killer for my business,” one Pennsylvania professional services owner wrote.
In a September survey of 1,600 decision-makers at U.S. businesses with fewer than 500 employees, ShipStation’s Q4 2026 Shipping Insights Report found that 52% named rising carrier fees and fuel surcharges as a major difficulty, up from 31% in its previous survey. Seventy-two percent said shipping and freight costs climbed in the past three months. ShipStation sells shipping software to small merchants.
Scale decides who can absorb it. Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, told TheStreet in an interview on holiday shipping costs for Main Street retailers that because of carrier fuel surcharges, “many smaller merchants are not gonna be able to offer” free delivery.
Some sellers hold their shipping rates
Not every seller is passing the increase along. Sarah Melendy, who sells honey through Mountain Thyme Honey and Gifts in Troutville, Virginia, charges a flat $10 for shipping and plans to keep it through the holidays, she told Roanoke station WDBJ7 for its report on holiday shipping prices for local sellers .
“I have seen an increase in prices, but not so drastic that it’s, you know, going to ruin my business,” Melendy said.
For one seller, the question heading into peak is whether to reopen at all. The seller, who posts as @goldfishinabag_, wrote on X on Nov. 8 that the shop remains closed.
“i would really like to reopen my shop by december but shipping prices have gone up so much i don’t feel good about charging my awesome lovely kind customers for these exorbitant prices,” the seller wrote.
Why it matters: Small Etsy and eBay sellers must reset free-shipping minimums and label pricing before Jan. 17, when USPS makes its fuel surcharge permanent at 11% and raises Ground Advantage rates 5.9%. Those who don’t will absorb higher costs or risk lower conversion heading into peak.

source_document.body:
GlobalFoundries broke ground Friday on a roughly $10 billion semiconductor plant in Malta, New York, the first of two factories planned under a U.S.-Japan investment agreement. The chipmaker expects the first plant to begin operating in 2029.
What’s Related
Once it reaches full production, the new plant is expected to produce about 900,000 wafers a year. Wafers are thin discs on which manufacturers build chips. GlobalFoundries said the facility will use 300-millimeter wafers, about 12 inches across, to make chips for vehicles, industrial equipment, and communications infrastructure .
Japan is providing up to $21 billion in funding for the two-plant plan, and New York State is providing $570 million in incentives to help move the first plant forward. GlobalFoundries was selected in October to provide the manufacturing technology and run both facilities.
400,000 wafers per year
The roughly 400,000-square-foot plant will go up at GlobalFoundries’ existing Malta campus, which serves as its global headquarters. The company says the site is already permitted for the project and can use existing infrastructure to speed construction.
The existing Malta facility has annual capacity for about 400,000 wafers on the same 300-millimeter basis, according to GlobalFoundries. The first new plant alone is designed to add more than twice that much capacity. Japanese chipmaker Renesas said in October that it is already factoring the additional New York capacity into its own production plans.
Who will own and run the plants?
GlobalFoundries told investors that an entity owned by the U.S. and Japanese governments would own the facilities and their manufacturing equipment. GlobalFoundries would build and run the plants, provide the chipmaking technology, and manage day-to-day costs such as labor , utilities, and materials. The government-owned entity would receive revenue from wafer sales.
Second plant still needs approval
The second Malta plant would receive a separate investment of about $10 billion and add room to make another 900,000 wafers a year. If approved and built, the two new facilities would together have annual capacity for about 1.8 million wafers at full production. GlobalFoundries gave a 2029 target for the first plant and has yet to announce a start date for the second.
GlobalFoundries estimates that the two-plant project would create more than 1,000 manufacturing jobs and about 27,000 jobs across construction and related businesses in New York’s Capital Region. The company says it is working with schools, colleges, and workforce development groups to train people for semiconductor manufacturing jobs.

source_document.body:
Most senior decision-makers in a recent energy-industry survey think today’s electricity demand forecasts are too low. The poll, commissioned for ADIPEC, which bills itself as “the world’s largest energy event,” found that 81% of 1,528 respondents expect artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand to exceed current forecasts, and 32% expect it to be much higher. The harder question is whether the wires, transformers, and permits will be ready if demand does.
A separate study, The Energy Readiness Equation from engineering and consulting firm Jacobs, puts numbers on that gap. Among 600 energy-sector decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, Singapore, and Australia, 71% said sufficient capital is available in their geography. Only 29% said there is both enough capital and enough investable projects. In the U.S., one in five said their organization consistently delivers major infrastructure on time and on budget, compared with 30% globally, and 80% ranked permitting and consenting among their three biggest barriers. ADIPEC’s respondents pointed to a related choke point: Delays in building and connecting grids were the second-biggest barrier to meeting demand after geopolitics, with supply chain and equipment constraints close behind.
That raises a question the industry has been slow to ask: How much more can the infrastructure already in the ground carry? State regulators are beginning to write that question into formal proceedings.
The NC Clean Energy Technology Center’s 50 States of Grid Modernization report for the third quarter of 2026 counted 411 grid modernization actions across 43 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico. The tally includes dockets and proposals as well as enacted policy, so it measures activity rather than results. The first trend the authors identify is a push for metrics and planning rules on “grid utilization,” which they define as how efficiently a utility uses its existing infrastructure to serve load.
Virginia lawmakers were the first in the country to order grid utilization metrics earlier this year, according to the report, and others are following. California enacted a bill that makes utility data on utilization opportunities public and requires utilities to assess whether such solutions can be cost-effective alternatives within distribution planning. Minnesota regulators ordered Xcel Energy to build utilization metrics into its next Integrated Distribution Plan. Colorado regulators opened a rulemaking under which distribution system plans must include a scenario that uses load flexibility to increase capacity utilization.
Flexible interconnection is the practical counterpart. Xcel Energy has filed a proposal in Colorado that would offer both static and dynamic flexible interconnection. Customers could enroll temporarily until the company completes system upgrades, or permanently as their long-term connection method. On the transmission side, New Jersey enacted a law requiring utilities to consider advanced transmission technologies in transmission project applications, with third-party cost-effectiveness testing to justify any decision to exclude them. Ohio regulators approved a cost-effectiveness methodology that counts reduced system losses and avoided upgrades, and Indiana regulators published a study covering nine categories of the technologies.
“Policymakers are increasingly interested in advanced transmission technologies, which allow utilities to improve usage of the grid without having to replace the existing infrastructure,” Brian Lips, a senior project manager at the center, said in a release accompanying the report.
The Jacobs report offers an example of the approach in practice. Guy Nicholson, head of zero carbon grid solutions at Statkraft, argues that connection constraints can reflect conservative assumptions, historic network data, or standardized processes rather than an absolute physical limit. By examining the network data, equipment capability, and operating conditions behind a connection offer, and working through those constraints with the system operator, Statkraft shortened the initial connection timeline for a battery project from seven years to two, according to the report. Part of the solution was accepting that the facility could be curtailed during the limited periods when the constraint genuinely arose.
“Once you understand what’s happening on the network, you can start to solve the problem from an engineering point of view: where does it overload, how do we protect it, and what can we do about it?” Nicholson said in the report.
That cuts both ways. A flexible connection trades some firmness for time, and the trade is easier to make when the system has room to spare. Jacobs notes that rapid load growth is eroding that room. “The resilience preparedness gap is real and gets much bigger as the system gets tighter,” Will Hazelip, U.S. president of National Grid, said in the Jacobs report.
The survey data suggest the gap is already visible. About 95% of Jacobs’ respondents said they are somewhat or very confident their critical assets would keep operating through a major disruption tomorrow, yet only 36% described their approach to resilience as proactive and embedded. The report also cautions that optimizing exclusively for speed can push economics, efficiency, resilience, and emissions down the decision hierarchy.
None of this replaces new generation, new lines, and new equipment, and none of those will arrive as fast as buyers want. But the questions commissions are starting to ask can be acted on now: How hard is the existing grid working, and where is capacity sitting idle?
Jacobs frames the shift as a move from asking “When can this project receive an unconstrained connection?” to “What can be connected safely now, and under what conditions?” The second question is the more useful one. The test will be whether utilities, regulators, and large loads accept the conditions that come with the answer, and whether anyone keeps an honest count of what the curtailed hours cost.
—Aaron Larson is POWER’s executive editor.

source_document.body:
EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
1979 Chevy SS Monte Mino Mixes El Camino, Monte Carlo SS, and Corvette, It'll Be a Hot Wheels Car
32 photos
Photo: Mattel
The worlds of cars and toys have always been intertwined, thanks to the few companies that have made it their lives' purpose to shrink and replicate real-world vehicles for fun and games in the hands of kids and adults alike. Usually, these toy makers treat us, on a constant basis, to replicas of existing production models, but, in some cases, they do go the extra mile and launch toys based on much rarer custom cars.
And by that I mostly mean Mattel, whose Hot Wheels brand has always produced cars and (at times) motorcycles like no others in the world. Most of them are, of course, based on production vehicles or even made up, but ever since 2018 the company has been treating us to exquisite four-wheelers based on some of the most insane custom builds in the world.
It was six years ago when the company launched the Legends Tour presented by Mobil 1, as a means to celebrate its 50th anniversary. The event kicked off as a U.S.-based competition backed by Walmart that sought to find extreme custom builds worthy of being turned into die-cast toys.
The idea caught on very rapidly and, more importantly than that, grew into something Hot Wheels now describes as the world’s largest traveling car show and global custom car competition. And you only need to look at this year's edition to quickly understand what that means.
Photo: Mattel For the 2026 Hot Wheels Legends Tour, the company's reps and their backers traveled to no less than 19 countries (in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Latin America, and Asia Pacific) in their search for the most exquisite build, stopping no less than 12 times in North America alone.
At dedicated events, Hot Wheels designers and local automotive experts had their say on each entry in the competition, evaluating them based on a number of criteria, including authenticity, creativity, and garage spirit.
The company does not specifically say how many entries had to be judged, but we do know which came on top at the end of it all: a 1979 Chevrolet El Camino put together by Tampa-based custom-car builder Matt McEntegart.
Ok, calling this thing an El Camino is a gross understatement, as the build process required the mounting of the coupe utility vehicle's body on a modified 2008 Corvette chassis stretched by 12 inches (30 cm), and fitting it with Monte Carlo SS widebody components. When all was said and done, a modified Chevrolet V8 engine of undisclosed capabilities was stuck under the hood.
Photo: Mattel For that reason, the car as you see it in the attached gallery is nicknamed SS Monte Mino, and it required thousands of hours of work to come together, all of them completed by McEntegart himself.
The result is a mutant vehicle dressed in maroon paint with red-tinted forged carbon fiber panels designed to replicate the look and feel of a Hot Wheels diecast. It rides on massive 22-inch wheels tied to a custom suspension system which allows it to sit uncomfortably close to the ground.
The interior is custom too, as you can't have one without the other, with the design of the cabin meant to evoke 1980s styling and mix it with modern-day Corvette technology.
After declaring the SS Monte Mino the winner of the 2026 Hot Wheels Legends Tour over the past weekend, the toy maker announced it will shrink it down and turn it into a 1:64-scale die-cast collectible that will be available all over the world. On top of that, the custom car will also get its place in the Hot Wheels Garage of Legends.
Photo: Mattel It's not yet clear when the newcomer will become available, but it probably won't be that long, if we are to judge by how things unfolded in the past. As a side note, this is the first time an entry from the United States was declared a winner since the 2022 edition.
Not far behind McEntegart and his design, this year's Hot Wheels competition registered runner-ups Sandranto Hertanu (Achun Owen) from Indonesia, with a 1961 Morris Mini turned into a pickup truck, Italian Andrea Cionco with a widebody 1990 Mazda MX-5, and Chilean Andres Romero Maureira, who entered the 1992 Chevrolet Salaya SP purpose-built race car animated by a V8 good for 450 hp.
I just had to mention these other three designs, as I'll try to dig up as much information as possible about them and bring them before you in all their juicy form in upcoming stories.

source_document.body:
Truckload rates were up big again in October with shipment counts extending a positive streak to three months, according to a Monday report from Cass Information Systems. The outsized rate gains are allowing one-way fleets to quickly repair margins, while fleets under dedicated arrangements have been slower to offset cost inflation.
Cass’ TL linehaul index, which tracks rates excluding fuel and accessorial surcharges, increased 0.9% from September and 9.9% year over year. The linehaul index is historically heavily weighted to for-hire contract rates but also includes spot market rates.
October marked the 22nd straight y/y increase. The dataset was 13.2% higher on a two-year-stacked comparison, which mitigates the noise embedded in prior-year comps and shows the momentum of change.
October 2026 | y/y | 2-year | m/m | m/m (SA)
Shipments | 5.9% | -2.3% | -0.6% | 1.7%
Expenditures | 26.5% | 26.3% | 1.0% | 2.9%
TL Linehaul Index | 9.9% | 13.2% | 0.9% | NM
Table: Cass Information Systems (SA – seasonally adjusted)
Cost pressures were evident in third-quarter TL carrier results, however, one-way fleets are logging large contractual rates gains after a multiyear downturn.
Knight-Swift Transportation ( NYSE: KNX ), which has 70% of its TL fleet operating under non-dedicated agreements, is now targeting “at least double-digit increases.” The company’s new bid season began earlier this month, and it continues to reap the benefits from its elevated spot market exposure. The carrier placed more units under non-contractual arrangements early in the year to more quickly take advantage of a crackdown on noncompliant capacity .
It said on its third-quarter call last month that internal tender rejections were running two to three times higher than the industry average, and that the rates it was receiving on transactional business were also above-market.
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
SONAR: Contract Rate Change Direction (CRCD.USA). The dataset measures the average percentage difference between new and former contract base rates. Recent contract renewals are averaging 13%.
Freight shipments captured by Cass increased 5.9% y/y in October, a third straight y/y increase after 42 months of declines. Shipments slipped 0.6% from September but increased 1.7% when seasonally adjusted. October marked the smallest decline on a two-year-stacked comparison in three years.
All domestic transportation modes are included in the index, with TL and less-than-truckload shipments representing the bulk of the dataset.
The report said that modest growth in retail and the industrial economy , along with IEEPA tariff refunds, was supporting freight demand. However, it said, “demand will be limited by elevated inflation and rising interest rates squeezing consumers and businesses,” and noted that tariff refunds will only have a temporary impact.
Cass’ shipments index is forecast to increase 3% y/y in November if typical seasonal patterns hold.
Cass’ expenditures index, which measures total freight spend including fuel, jumped 26.5% y/y, up 2.9% seasonally adjusted from September. This was the highest growth rate for the index since July 2022, the tail end of the boom cycle.
Higher transportation rates and fuel surcharges, along with the increase in shipment counts, are driving the surge in freight spend. Retail diesel prices were 70% higher y/y in October. Cass’ expenditures index is forecast to increase by 24% y/y in November.
“We continue to see the freight demand cycle gaining steam, and with record container imports and intermodal volumes, and growing LTL tonnage, the improvement has broadened out some in recent months,” the report said.
Data used in the indexes comes from freight bills paid by Cass ( NASDAQ: CASS ). Cass processes $37 billion in freight payables annually on behalf of customers.
Why it matters? October data from Cass highlights a continued surge in TL contract rates alongside only modestly improved freight demand. The dataset confirms the impact strict regulatory enforcement is having on non-compliant capacity.

source_document.body:
FedEx Corp. has expanded its footprint at Guangzhou Baiyun Airport with the opening of a new cargo terminal, giving it more capacity in South China’s heavy industrial belt to support regional and international trade flows.
FedEx ( NYSE: FDX ) said Monday it pursued the facility expansion because of growing air cargo demand from shippers in the Greater Bay area, one of the world’s most heavily concentrated manufacturing hubs. The region, which includes Macau, Hong Kong and nine cities in Guangdong province, is one of the largest export centers in the world. In the first three quarters of 2026, the region’s nine mainland cities recorded imports and exports of $1.26 trillion, accounting for 21% of China’s total trade, according to China Customs.
The air logistics warehouse complements FedEx’s existing Asia-Pacific hub at Baiyun Airport, which opened in 2009. FedEx said it would help southern China businesses reach overseas customers and suppliers faster through its global air and ground network.
The 484,000-square foot facility, developed in tandem with the Guangdong Airport Authority to handle up 28,000 express parcels and freight shipments per hour, has three times the previous processing capacity thanks to intelligent sorting capabilities. Annual cargo handling capacity exceeds 110,000 U.S. tons. Other features include automation, RFID shipment tracking and a customs-supervised warehouse. The “smart” warehouse is supported by digital documentation, pre-declarations and alert systems to further reduce clearance times for customers.
FedEx CEO Raj Subramaniam attended the opening ceremony, according to the South China Morning Post.
“The future of trade depends on reliable connectivity, resilient supply chains, and access to global markets,” said Salil Chari, president, Asia Pacific, FedEx, in a news release. “The Greater Bay Area remains one of the most dynamic economic regions in the world, and this investment reinforces our commitment to helping businesses in China and across Asia-Pacific grow internationally. By strengthening connectivity and integrating this facility into our global network, we are enabling customers to move goods more efficiently, reach new markets, and seize emerging opportunities in global trade.”
FedEx continues to invest in airport infrastructure projects in the past 18 months, even as it decreases overall capital expenditure as part of an effort to reduce excess network capacity and improve profitability. The freight transportation giant this month completed an upgrade of its air facility in Madrid, Spain . In February, the company announced plans to build a new air logistics hub in Mumbai, India . FedEx moved to a new terminal at Istanbul airport in Turkey in September 2025. It also announced plans to invest in a new air cargo hub in Saudi Arabia .
UPS is similarly upgrading its Asia air network, having recently completed a new air hub in the Philippines while construction continues on a major expansion of its air hub in Hong Kong.
