source_document.body:
presented by
Smaller radars are taking on a larger role in air-and-missile defense, including tactical radars that can be mounted on mobile units. (Photo courtesy of Leonardo DRS RADA.)
Missile and drone attacks in Ukraine and the Middle East are putting new pressure on the radars that underpin air-and-missile defense, driving demand for systems that can be fielded faster, in greater numbers, and be networked across a wider area.
Breaking Defense spoke with Joe Mollo, senior director of Advanced Programs at Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit (DRS RADA), about surging demand for tactical radars, the push to expand manufacturing capacity, and how a new generation of sensors could change the way air defenses are built.
Breaking Defense: There’s been a lot of attention in Washington on defense-industrial base capacity and resilience, particularly in response to the new threats we’re facing in the CENTCOM region. Summarize what you view as the rapidly evolving threat?
Mollo: The Iranian-designed Shahed/Geran loitering munition has become the poster-child of this new threat environment, and it’s evolving on multiple axes at once. In Ukraine, we’ve seen single-day tactical drone employment exceed 10,000 units along the front line, while the long-range strike variant aimed at cities has simultaneously gone jet-powered – now representing over half of deep-strike sorties, shortening the already challenging warning time of the original propeller-driven design, requiring a defense that detects sooner, engages further, and acts faster.
Joe Mollo, senior director of Advanced Programs, Leonardo DRS RADA
Against Israel, we’ve now seen three massive, coordinated Iranian state barrages – April 2024, October 2024, and the 12-day war in June 2025 – each launching hundreds to over a thousand ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones directly from Iranian soil. Layer on top of that the grinding, continuous fire from Iran’s proxies: 15,000-20,000-plus rockets, missiles, and drones from Hezbollah and the Houthis. The threat is constant and pervasive, requiring a defense that scales, costs less, and is mobile.
Operation Epic Fury and the parallel Houthi Red Sea campaign showed this threat has outgrown any single theater. Iran demonstrated both the willingness and the reach to strike across the entire Gulf – and, more troubling for us, the ability to take out major US IAMD sensor infrastructure.
Ballistic missiles and low-cost one-way attack drones together damaged or destroyed radar systems in Qatar, Jordan, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, and Kuwait – including a $1.1 billion early-warning radar. Those systems will take years to replace.
This requires a defense that can be produced faster and has a cost that supports dispersed operations for survivability. Such systems need to look at things that are low and slow or low and fast, the cruise missiles, the Group 3 drones. Tactical radars for survivability’s sake and the ability to look low have become a real hot item. If you’re going to have a big radar protecting a geographic area and that’s the first thing that gets hit, well now I need smaller, more dispersed radar capabilities.
The real issue is whether the US industrial base produces sensor and interceptor systems at the quantity and speed that this evolving threat demands in order to protect US and allied interests.
Mobile radars are harder for adversary forces to target and can be moved as needed to provide coverage across a wider area. (Photo courtesy of Leonardo DRS RADA.)
How does this translate to DRS RADA?
As a leading global supplier of tactical radar systems for counter-UAS, air-defense, and missile-defense applications, DRS RADA is feeling the stress of significant demand across both US and international markets. In the United States, demand is increasing from the Department of War and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as through Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Direct Commercial Sales (DCS) to international partners.
DRS RADA also continues to see sustained demand from customers in the Middle East and Eastern Europe served through its non-US operations. This is reflected in record bookings in each of the past two quarters, underscoring both the breadth and urgency of this demand.
Ukraine came in at the end of 2023 with a single order in which they ordered more than we had sold the prior two years. All of a sudden we’re getting this tremendous demand for tactical radars.
Additionally, there is an increased emphasis on robust homeland missile defense, especially in light of the operational lessons demonstrating the vulnerability of our current inventory of long-range sensors. Looking at the Golden Dome concept, these expensive radars, which are necessary for your long-range ballistic missiles, are the first to be hit. And, oh by the way, they take four or five years to produce and cost half a billion to a billion dollars.
In response, we looked at any way we can use smaller tactical radars in a disaggregated way. This would include geographically dispersed sensors that are more affordable and manufacturable at scale, that can be networked to provide the coverage, resilience, and mission performance traditionally associated with a few exquisite systems. DRS RADA’s tactical radar portfolio is well aligned with this shift toward disaggregated, networked sensing.
DRS RADA also supports numerous prime contractors and system integrators that are responding to the same market demand. These customers require close engineering and program support to integrate DRS RADA radar systems into complete mission solutions spanning the detect-to-effect chain. As a result, growth in radar-unit demand is accompanied by increased requirements for product development, systems integration, technical support, and manufacturing resources.
Together, these dynamics – higher demand volumes, shorter delivery timelines, and increasingly challenging customer requirements – are driving substantial investment in accelerated product development and expanded manufacturing and test capacity.
How is DRS RADA addressing the surge in demand?
The 2022 merger with Leonardo DRS has been instrumental in enabling the company to scale in response to growing customer demand. This merger has enabled us to increase R&D investment to accelerate new-product development, capitalize expanded manufacturing and test capacity, and add the technical and business infrastructure needed to build and sustain a global presence.
DRS RADA currently manufactures six radar models spanning a range of sizes, power levels, and missions. We continue to sustain and advance these models through ongoing improvements informed by requirements derived from extensive operational deployments. For example, these changes may support new technical requirements, such as new electronic counter-countermeasures, ECCM, threats and integration requirements.
DRS RADA is releasing two new radar models this month, the result of significant R&D investment and extensive development, integration, and testing over the past several years.
In terms of capital investment, the company has committed to expanding capacity in the communities that have supported our growth, while leveraging its broader international footprint to strengthen the supply chain for critical materials. At our Germantown, Maryland, facility, RADA has expanded its engineering and manufacturing workforce from 30 to 150 employees with 60 more planned for early 2027.
Our footprint has increased nearly 10-fold and our complex test facilities by four times. We are planning another wave of expansion to accommodate our newest product, the cxMHR (RPS-502), which is larger and more complex than any of our other systems, requiring its own dedicated production and test facilitation. And we’ve got another expansion following what we’re doing right now.
We’ve been in Montgomery County for the entire time we’ve been in the US and we wanted to stay there, stay there with the people that have worked with us all that time, stay with the community that supported us. So we’ve made all that investment right at home in Germantown, Maryland.
However, our global development and manufacturing footprint has undertaken expansion across our multiple facilities similar in scale to our US operations. These facilities are located in operational areas of conflict or where regional restrictions require a physical presence. One of the benefits of this distributed manufacturing footprint is that it improves DRS RADA’s supply-chain resilience and cost efficiency by enabling each location to source appropriate materials from its respective regional market, which can then be made available company wide, reducing dependence on any single supplier base or geography.
What does the cxMHR bring operationally?
As I noted earlier, the cxMHR is significantly larger, more powerful, and more complex than our other radar models and represents a major technology step forward that delivers a clear operational advantage in the medium-range tactical radar market.
The cxMHR operates in C-band, which occupies a very useful middle ground. It provides the high-resolution and precision-tracking performance typically associated with higher-frequency X-band systems while offering range and weather benefits similar to S-band.
What is particularly unique and important is that the cxMHR uses a fully digital aperture. Like all of our radars, the cxMHR is a software-defined active electronically scanned array (AESA) system. AESA is the current state of the art for tactical radars, giving users tremendous flexibility to tailor performance for a specific mission or to support multiple missions simultaneously, all through software control. This is particularly important for evolving missions or multi-mission requirements and for resilience against electronic attack.
AESA technology represents a meaningful distinction from both conventional phased-array and metamaterial-based approaches. A conventional passive phased-array radar relies on a centralized transmitter and phase control across the aperture, which provides electronic beam steering, but less independent control over the individual radiating elements and less flexibility to generate or manage multiple, mission-specific functions simultaneously. Metamaterial apertures performance is far less effective in mitigating electronic attack because it is closely linked to the electromagnetic response of the physical surface and requires iterative aperture-specific optimization to achieve a particular use case.
With a fully digital array, the cxMHR takes AESA another step forward. The cxMHR’s fully digital AESA architecture provides true, independent, per-element control across the transmit/receive aperture. This gives the radar exceptional ability to tailor beams, waveforms, power distribution, and radar-resource allocation rapidly and repeatedly via digital control.
The operational advantages are profound. These include: up to 40 times faster volume scan; precision beam pointing, a narrower main beam, less SNR loss, longer detection range, and less multi-path interference; simultaneous search, track, and jammer localization beams; ECCM and EMI performance with less clutter and better jamming suppression; independent element calibration and control for less loss and graceful degradation; and frequency diversity for reduced multipath elevation errors and reduced RCS fluctuation, resulting in a higher Pd.
If it gets shot, you’re not going to take out half of the radar. You’re going to take out maybe one of these elements, maybe four of them. The radar will still continue to work. It’s not a spinner. It gives you the whole 360-degree constant view, and there’s no moving parts in the antenna assembly.
In terms of dealing with jammers and interference from other sources, there’s less clutter and more resistance to jamming.
With true per-element digital control, the cxMHR can make mission-driven adjustments through digital control in a faster, more repeatable, and more deterministic manner.
What are your thoughts on the future of DRS RADA?
DRS RADA is well positioned to help the United States and its allies address the rapidly evolving threats we’re seeing in the CENTCOM region and future battlespaces. Since entering the tactical radar market eight years ago, DRS RADA has consistently invested in technology, product performance, and responsiveness to operational user requirements.
From its first prototype, DRS RADA has designed its radars around gallium nitride (GaN) technology and software-defined AESA architectures. GaN enables higher performance in a smaller, lighter, and more power-efficient package than legacy gallium arsenide based (GaAs) systems. While the US continues to pay for vendors to upgrade its tactical-radar inventory from GaAs to GaN, DRS RADA’s radar portfolio was designed around GaN from the outset.
Equally important, DRS RADA’s products have been shaped by extensive operational experience and direct user feedback. It wouldn’t be out of the realm of possibility to say that more of our radars have been shot than some of our competitors have ever produced. We continue to sustain and advance our radar models through extensive R&D investment, incorporating improvements that address evolving mission requirements and emerging threats.
DRS RADA has always operated under a startup mentality with continuous innovation. It’s served us really well and it continues to serve us really well because our adversaries have that same pace of change.
DRS RADA radars led the way for US capabilities in mobile short-range air defense, counter-UAS, and active protection system missions. Building on that foundation, the company continues to deliver high-performing tactical radars and develop integrated sensor solutions that help warfighters detect, track, and respond to the new and evolving threats they face in battle.
That last quarter that just ended was a record breaker like none we’ve ever seen. The quarter before that was a record breaker like none that we’ve ever seen. It just doesn’t stop; the demand just keeps coming.

source_document.body:
A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.
Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and says it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data .
What happened on Golden Gate Parkway
At 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.
The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
FHP said the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.
What Tesla told the federal government
Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.
It identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph , a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.
This record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.
Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports .
How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.
Tesla has the video
Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.
So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.
Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?
There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.
Two in Naples
This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.
The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.
Electrek’s Take
This is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.
We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.
If FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.
We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland . How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

You’ll Never Believe How Much The F15 BMW X5 Now Costs. It’s Pennies on the Dollar!
15 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
If you want a BMW X5 in your life but don’t fancy the new generation due to its Neue Klasse design inside and out, not to mention the fact that it comes from a minimum of $69,800 (MSRP) in its most basic version, the RWD X5 40, then this would be a good time to search the used car market for an older one.
The G05 can cost between $20,000 and upward of $85,000, depending the mileage, trim level, powertrain, and overall condition. And if you are unfamiliar with the codenames, then you should know that this is the predecessor of the modern-day (G65) Neue Klasse BMW X5. It was made from 2018 to 2026, and it does not show its age yet, this writer thinks.
Is the G05 out of your budget? Then how about its predecessor, the F15 ? This one was made between 2013 and 2018. Production took place not only at the South Carolina factory in USA, but also in Russia, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Egypt. It shared plenty of nuts and bolts with the era’s 5 Series, namely the G30, as well as the old X6 (F16). And it costs between $10,000 and over $40,000 in today’s used car market in USA.
Paying a little over $10,000 would get you an earlier model year, whereas the mid-range model year versions tend to fetch from $15,000 to over $25,000. The range-topping X5 M from this generation generally costs in the region of $20,000, and features a 4.4L twin-turbo V8 with 567 hp (423 kW/575 ps) and 553 lb-ft (750 Nm) of torque, hitting 62 mph (100 kph) in 4.2 seconds.
Photo: Cars&Bids Pictured above is not the X5 M , but an xDrive35i from the 2014 model year. This BMW X5 has 300 horsepower (224 kW/304 ps) and 300 lb-ft (407 Nm) of torque on tap, and power comes from the N55 unit, a 3.0-liter turbocharged straight-six engine. This model uses an eight-speed automatic transmission that sends the output to the xDrive all-wheel drive system, and needed around 6.5 seconds to hit 62 mph (100 kph) from zero.
In the North American market, the top speed was electronically limited to 130 mph (210 kph), and overseas market cars could reach 146 mph (235 kph). By the way, Europe’s X5 from this era, in the xDrive35i configuration, had 302 hp (225 kW/306 ps) and 295 lb-ft (400 Nm) of torque to play with.
The pictured BMW X5 had a little over 58,000 miles (~93,400 km) on the clock at the time of cataloging. It is presented in Mineral White Metallic on top of an Ivory White interior. The M Sport Package, Driver Assistance Plus Package, Nappa leather upholstery, a panoramic sunroof, power-adjustable front seats with heating and ventilation, a four-zone automatic climate control system, and a Bang & Olufsen premium sound system are mentioned in the ad as being part of the equipment.
Mind you, not everything is perfect, because the SUV in question has chips and scratches on the outside, a scuff on the front bumper, a ding on the tailgate, weathered finish on the exterior trim, and curb rash on the wheels. The wear on the door cards and interior touch points, as well as wear on the front seat bolsters are also mentioned in the ad. Moreover, this ride was involved in two accidents, in August 2021 and January 2024, sustaining “minor” damage in both cases.
Photo: Cars&Bids This BMW X5 has a clean California title. It had its engine oil and filter changed in February 2026, at 57,147 miles (91,969 km), as well as in December 2024, at 50,844 miles (81,825 km). In the latter date, it also had its cabin air filter replaced, the brake fluid flushed, the engine oil filter adapter replaced, and got new spark plugs.
In January 2024, the outside mirror was repaired/replaced, the brake fluid flushed, engine oil and filter changed, rear brake pads and rotors replaced, and tires rotated. The battery was replaced in July 2023, and in November 2022, at 22,675 miles (36,492 km), the SUV had its engine oil and filter changed, and the brake fluid flushed, the listing shows.
According to the ad, the selling dealer reportedly bought this BMW X5 in July 2026, and they recently parted ways with it. The vehicle was accompanied by two keys and nothing else, and it literally went for pennies on the dollar compared to what it initially cost. We don’t know how much the first owner paid for it, but let’s not forget that this model used to retail for over $56,000 back then, and this is a nicely-equipped example with plenty of extras.
The selling price was $11,611, as that’s how much it got at the end of the online auction on Cars&Bids, which concluded on November 13, 2026. The SUV was advertised at no reserve, and you can check it out in more detail here . But before you do, let us know if you would have made it yours for that sum.

SolarEdge Technologies has launched the company’s Duo Power Optimizer for commercial and industrial (C&I) solar installations in the U.S. The company made the announcement November 16 ahead of the RE+ renewable energy conference in Las Vegas, Nevada.
The company said the Duo “delivers the same module-level energy harvest as a one-to-one power optimizer with half as many units to specify, wire and install, connecting two modules to one optimizer with an independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT) for each.” The group said the technology “also features SolarEdge’s innovative Arc Fault Detection, a global industry first that uses every optimizer as an arc sensor to detect arcs at the source rather than only at the inverter.”
SolarEdge said that in a traditional string inverter system, the weakest module drags the output of the entire string, and the gap widens as modules degrade at different rates. With optimizers, an underperforming module affects only its own output.
“The bottom line is true module-level energy harvesting and visibility, with fewer optimizers to buy, wire and install,” said Gokul Krishnan, SVP and general manager, North America at SolarEdge. “We also added safety features no one else in the industry has, including arc fault detection at the optimizer level. That addresses blind spots in the array where traditional string inverters can’t detect an arc. And the way we’ve designed the inputs gives installers real improvements in wire management on site.”
Sense Connect Technology
SolarEdge said the Duo extends Sense Connect technology to every input and output connector, monitoring temperature to flag developing faults before an overheating connector can lead to an arc. The company said that “with every Power Optimizer acting as an individual arc sensor, detection is distributed across the array instead of relying on a single point at the inverter, so if one optimizer misses an arc, its neighbor can catch it. Detecting close to where an arc can form enhances accuracy and sensitivity, helping stop an arc before it escalates. Protection covers strings with up to 3,280 feet (1,000 meters) of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer, and issues are pinpointed down to the optimizer area for quick, cost-effective resolution.”
Each optimizer has two input pairs: a short pair for the closest module, and a pre-extended pair for the adjacent one, reducing wire slack and eliminating field-made jumpers. Because one optimizer can connect two modules facing different azimuth angles, the Duo suits dual-tilt racking.
The Duo, which is manufactured in Florida, is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and FEOC (Foreign Entity of Concern) requirements and is expected to ship to international markets in 2027.
“We saw a clear difference in wire management on the roof, with fewer connections to make and no extra jumpers to run, which saved our crews real time during installation,” said Aaron Wilson, CEO of Solar One. “SolarEdge did an excellent job with the extension lengths, leaving very little excess wiring for our crews to manage. With the Duo, installers get module-level visibility with 50% fewer optimizers than one-to-one designs like the C651U. Being able to monitor performance down to the individual module gives us greater confidence in the system’s long-term output and makes troubleshooting far more precise when we do need to return to the site.”
SolarEdge is showcasing the Duo at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, Nov. 17-19, with shipments expected to begin in January 2027.
— Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.

source_document.body:
The 2,488-carat Motswedi diamond. ( Image courtesy of Lucara Diamond. )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie November 16, 2026
Lucara Diamond (TSX: LUC) has raised its annual revenue forecast by 30% at the midpoint after sales of two giant diamonds from its Karowe mine in Botswana boosted returns amid continued weakness in smaller stones.
The Vancouver-based miner now expects full-year revenue of $140 million to $160 million (C$200 million to C$228 million), up from its previous guidance of $100 million to $130 million, Lucara said Nov. 13.
“Lucara Diamond reported better-than-expected operational metrics, largely due to higher throughput,” BMO Capital Markets mining analyst Raj Ray said in a Nov. 16 note. “Revenue improved due to the sale of the 1,303-carat diamond, hence revenue guidance has been lifted.”
The higher revenue outlook and lower operating-cost forecast offer support as Lucara develops Karowe’s underground expansion, which is expected to reach full-scale production in the first half of 2028. The company’s reliance on exceptional stones also leaves quarterly results sensitive to the timing of individual sales.
The 2,488-carat Motswedi diamond was sold in the second quarter, while the 1,303-carat stone was recovered and sold in the third quarter. Both contributed to the annual guidance increase.
Third-quarter revenue rose 19% year on year to $61.1 million, well above BMO’s $33.3-million forecast, as sales volumes increased 12% to 113,227 carats. Net profit slipped 11% to $6.6 million from $7.4 million a year earlier.
Lucara shares gained 25% to C14¢ by mid-Monday in Toronto, valuing the company at nearly C$206 million.
Large diamond sales
Sales to Belgian manufacturer HB Trading, which buys Karowe’s gem and near-gem diamonds weighing more than 10.8 carats, jumped 28% to $48.5 million. The arrangement accounted for 79% of quarterly revenue.
Revenue from regular tenders held at $11.2 million as higher sales volumes offset an 11% decline in average prices. Revenue from Lucara’s diamond sales through the Clara digital platform fell 30% to $1.4 million, largely reflecting a 26% drop in average prices per carat.
The lower Clara prices reflected a greater proportion of smaller, lower-quality diamonds from stockpiled ore and continued pricing pressure on smaller goods, Lucara said.
Lucara sold Clara to a group led by former CEO Eira Thomas and HRA Group in 2024, while entering a five-year rough-diamond supply agreement that allowed termination after its second anniversary. Lucara has given notice to end the agreement on Dec. 22 and will shift those sales to regular tenders in the first quarter of 2027.
Karowe expansion
Total production declined 0.9% to 96,767 carats, comprising 94,067 carats from direct ore feed and 2,700 carats recovered from historical tailings. Alongside the 1,303-carat stone, recoveries included a 316-carat diamond and seven stones weighing between 100 and 200 carats.
Lucara lowered its annual operating-cost forecast to $24 to $26 per tonne processed, from $27.50 to $31. Quarterly costs were $22.41 per tonne, below BMO’s $29 estimate, as higher throughput and lower in-pit mining activity offset increased power costs.
The underground expansion moved from shaft construction to lateral development during the quarter. Lucara spent $40.7 million on the project, with $245.2 million remaining to complete it at Sept. 30, including contingency.
Naseem Lahri, managing director of Lucara’s Botswana operations, will leave that role on Nov. 30. She will continue supporting the transition through the end of the first quarter of 2027.
Market outlook
Global natural diamond production is forecast to fall below 100 million carats in 2026, compared with more than 150 million carats less than a decade ago, as ageing mines become depleted and producers suspend or close operations, Lucara said.
Larger, rarer stones have shown stronger price performance, supported by constrained supply and resilient demand, while smaller commercial diamonds remain under pressure from economic uncertainty and competition from lab-grown alternatives, the company said. Synthetic diamond prices have continued to decline as production capacity expands, it added.

EICMA 2026 • Here Are Some of the Serious and Obscure Brands That EICMA 2026 Had To Offer – Worth Knowing About
Mercedes Stops Individual Orders for the EQE Sedan, EQE SUV, and EQS SUV in Germany
10 photos
Photo: Mercedes-Benz
If you live in Germany and intend to configure an EQE Sedan today, I'm afraid you are too late. Mercedes-Benz Deutschland has quietly revised its online configurator, deleting the full-electric sedan and two EQS-branded sport utility vehicles in the process. The configurator informs prospective customers that said models are "no longer available for individual order," directing EQE Sedan, EQE SUV, and EQS SUV buyers to vehicles that are currently in stock.
Curiously enough, the EQS Sedan gets to stay. The German automaker from Stuttgart also revised it substantially for model year 2027, with updates including a steer-by-wire system and 800-volt goodies for a driving range of up to 926 kilometers (575 miles) in the WLTP for the rear-drive 450+ version.
Funny thing, Merc's ordering restrictions in the German market extend to a few additional European markets, including the United Kingdom, France, and the Netherlands. Even so, the Stuttgart-based manufacturer has yet to officially explain what is actually happening to these three models on the Old Continent.
Stopping individual orders is a different thing from ending series production, but looking at the bigger picture, Mercedes is preparing to replace them all. The E-Class with EQ Technology comes to mind, a mid-size electric sedan that will soon replace the EQE Sedan in the company's passenger vehicle lineup.
Both sedans and both sport utility vehicles are based on the Electric Vehicle Architecture, which is the automaker's first dedicated all-electric platform. Going forward, the passenger vehicle division will rely on two main platforms: MMA for compacts and MB.EA for midsizers. Then there's the AMG.EA of the GT 4-Door Coupe and its SUV-bodied sibling, whereas the van division flaunts the VAN.EA architecture for the luxury-oriented VLE and VLS.
Photo: Mercedes-AMG Mercedes launched the EVA-based EQS Sedan in 2021, followed by the EQE twins a year later. Together with the EQS SUV, they represented the company's failed attempt to establish a dedicated luxury-oriented electric vehicle family with styling distinct from their internal combustion counterparts.
I remember YouTuber Arun Maini, a.k.a. mrwhosetheboss, buying an EQS Sedan for his mom a few years ago. Unfortunately for Mercedes, not even this kind of exposure helped the EQS Sedan from a commercial standpoint. All four models fell flat on their faces, selling very few units in pretty much every market where Mercedes is present.
It got so bad in the United States of America that Mercedes pulled the plug on the EQE Sedan and EQE SUV there after only four years on the market. In any case, the EQS Sedan soldiers on with very desirable updates and figures, including a 13 percent driving range improvement over the pre-facelift.
Its 800-volt electrical system handles up to 350 kilowatts, allowing the full-size electric luxury sedan to recover 320 kilometers (199 miles) of WLTP driving range in 10 minutes. A larger battery is on the menu as well, along with new electric drive units developed from scratch rather than based on the previous drive units.
Mercedes also took inspiration from the Volkswagen Group with a two-speed transmission for the rear-mounted electric drive unit, allowing it to prioritize acceleration performance in first and efficiency in second. Speaking of taking inspiration, Mercedes also rolled out a yoke-type optional steering wheel that would make Tesla proud.

Rolls-Royce Pits Black Against White in Luxury Backgammon Set That Took a Year to Make
9 photos
Photo: Rolls-Royce
With Christmas shopping fever just around the corner, everybody everywhere is scrambling to get ready for what's to come. And I'm not only talking about customers, but the companies that will have something to offer in the months ahead as well. Like, say, British carmaker Rolls-Royce, which seems to have taken a break from making cars this winter and opted to release a backgammon set instead.
That's right, backgammon, the game that has been played by millions (possibly billions), be them aristocracy or addicted gamblers, ever since its early days, some 5,000 years ago, in its presumed point of origin, Mesopotamia.
Now, Rolls-Royce is no stranger to coming up from time to time with products that are anything but cars. You may remember how, in the spring of last year, it came out with a chess set that people with enough money in their bank accounts went nuts over. Probably, the Brits hope this will be the case with the backgammon game as well, especially with Christmas just around the corner.
Described as a playable work of art, the game does come across as being just as luxurious and exquisite as all other things Rolls-Royce. And I'm not talking solely about the materials that were used to make it, but about the way it looks and (probably) feels as well.
Made in-house by the company's Bespoke Collective, the Rolls-Royce backgammon set is made of the same materials and colors the company uses for its cars: ochre, stone, sand (all three meant to remind people of the landscapes of ancient Mesopotamia), aluminum, American walnut, natural grain leather – you name it.
Photo: Rolls-Royce The case itself is crafted from the kind of wood mentioned above, and decorated accordingly, but that's not what makes the board special. As you know, the backgammon case is foldable, and it is at the hinge that Rolls-Royce went nuts.
As a mechanism you'll see nowhere else, made from a solid billet of aluminum, hand-polished and then anodized, it is at the same time both functional and aesthetic. That's because the carmaker designed it in such a way as to rotate open while the central spine counter-rotates to bring into the spotlight the playing pieces and the crafted board.
Because this is a Rolls-Royce creation we're talking about, there is a Spirit of Ecstasy on deck, mounted to the said hinge in such a way that it orients itself regardless of the board's position. Kind of like the self-levelling wheel caps of the real Rolls cars usually do.
The central spine of the case is also where the precision dice, doubling die, and a pair of dice shakers are placed, as is the removable plinth where captured counters can be stored during the game.
Photo: Rolls-Royce When it comes to the playing surface itself, Rolls book-matched it at 55 degrees, just as it happens when it comes to the veneer application in car interiors. The materials used for it include open-pore royal walnut and smoked eucalyptus, among others.
The stones of the game, meaning the actual playing pieces, are made of an undisclosed composite with bauxite ore infusion, and come in Deep Night Sky black and Antarctica white, one color for each player.
Rolls seems to take great pride in the way the anodized aluminum doubling die has been designed, with its shape inspired by the honeycomb structures found in nature, but also the shape of nuts and bolts. The inspiration for this came first and foremost from the company's apiaries in Germany, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Qatar .
The final piece of this special backgammon set, the dice shakers, are made of machined aluminum as well, and finished to match the hinge. The bases are made of leather to smooth out the sound of the throw. As a final touch, the Spirit of Ecstasy is engraved beneath.
Photo: Rolls-Royce The reason why this backgammon set exists is not some wacky idea someone over at Rolls-Royce had, but the fact that this game has been tied to the carmaker before: back in 1938, for instance, a Wraith was commissioned with such a thing, built into the rear passenger compartment.
This time, it stands alone and can be purchased by anyone. Ok, maybe not anyone, but definitely the owners of Rolls-Royce cars. Although the company makes no mention of pricing, there is chatter of one such backgammon set selling for around $50,000, which accounts for the displayed level of luxury and takes into account the fact that it took about one year to develop.
Still, that's not nearly as steep as the most expensive backgammon set ever, the $5 million Charles Hollander, or the Geoffrey Parker super-enriched board ($387,000).
Offered at tournament size, the game is not yet listed online (unlike the chess set), but the British company says customers can already ask for one in showrooms and private offices.

BYD’s new, larger entry-level EV will go on sale in Europe, but it won’t be called the Dolphin Surf as expected.
BYD’s new Seagull EV to launch as the Dolphin in Europe
The Seagull is BYD’s smallest, most affordable electric car, starting at about $10,000 in China. In Europe and the UK, it’s sold as the Dolphin Surf, and in other overseas markets, it’s called the Dolphin Mini.
With over 245,000 Seagull (Dolphin Mini/ Dolphin Surf) models sold through September, it’s BYD’s most popular pure electric vehicle and among the top-selling EVs worldwide so far this year.
After launching the second-generation “Great” Seagull in China, a larger, more advanced version, BYD was expected to introduce it overseas as the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Apparently, that will not be the case. BYD will introduce the updated version overseas, but according to the Spanish media outlet TestCoches , it will replace the larger Dolphin hatch rather than the Dolphin Surf.
BYD second-generation Seagull EV (Source: Zhang Zhuo)
The second-generation model will offer BYD’s five-minute Flash Charging technology and Blade Batteries 2.0.
In China, the new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000). For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super Trade-In” promotion, bringing the starting price down to just 62,900 yuan ($9,500).
The second-gen Seagull measures 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than its predecessor.
Thanks to the added space, BYD’s new Seagull now offers room for five passengers, up from four in the outgoing version.
Instead of a front-wheel-drive powertrain, the new version switches to rear-wheel-drive. The setup uses a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from 55 kW (75 hp).
With BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. To go from 10% to 97% takes just nine minutes.
Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes just 3 minutes longer (12 minutes) to charge from 20% to 97%. However, Flash Charging is not included as standard on the two cheapest entry-level variants.
While the bigger dimensions and Flash Charging were the biggest updates, BYD also added a few premium extras.
To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.
Inside, BYD revamped the interior with its latest in-car software and technology. The new setup includes a larger 15.6″ center infotainment screen, a redesigned two-spoke steering wheel and center console with smart storage, plus added physical buttons.
All versions are equipped with BYD’s DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a 140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system.
The optional DiPilot 300 system with God’s Eye B intelligent driving assistance is available. It includes a roof-mounted LiDAR to provide ADAS features such as City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.
In China, BYD offers the new Seagull EV with two Blade 2.0 LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh. The former provides a CLTC range of up to 320 km (199 miles), while the latter provides up to 420 km (261 miles).
The current Dolphin Surf measures 3,990 mm in length, and the Dolphin is 4,290 mm long. Selling the updated version as the Dolphin makes more sense, given how much closer in size it is.
BYD will continue selling the Dolphin Surf in Spain and throughout Europe, with the updated model now featuring five seats and a few other key improvements.
In Europe, BYD’s Dolphin Surf starts at about €22,990 ($25,000), and the larger Dolphin is priced from around €33,990 ($37,500).

Man Buys 2026 Lexus LC 500 Convertible Inspiration Series for $120K, Adds 761 Miles, Sells for $147
31 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
Since this is America and everybody loves Lexus, it's no wonder that this barely-driven, limited edition LC 500 Convertible just sold at auction for roughly $27,000 over MSRP. While the seller didn't present a sticker, we know the MSRP on one of these babies came down to around $120,000 or so. So yeah, there's a quick $27k for you. Flipper heaven.
Despite the limited-edition factor, which is always highly desirable among collectors (and buyers in general), the LC500's calling card is still its 5.0-liter naturally aspirated V8 engine - one of the last naturally aspirated V8s available in a luxury grand tourer. It's not particularly powerful by modern standards, but it does offer that immediate throttle response and linear power curve that enthusiasts crave. Not to mention an incredible soundtrack as you approach 7,300 rpm.
Then there's the Toyota/Lexus reliability factor. Or reputation, I should say. This particular V8 engine is exceptionally reliable, and so is the LC 500, for something this expensive. As for the Inspiration Series spec, it's a swan song for the LC 500 , whose production is set to end in 2026 with no immediate direct replacement announced.
Let's take a closer look at what makes this particular car special, starting with the Wind colorway. It's very elegant and it works well together with the LC 500's design language. Other visual highlights include the convertible soft-top, triple-beam LED headlights, the flush door handles, a surround-view camera, front canards, a rear diffuser, PPF on the front fascia, plus a set of 21" forged wheels with Michelin rubber and Lexus-branded calipers.
Meanwhile, inside is where you'll find the white and Saddle Tan leather upholstery, heated, ventilated, and power-adjustable front sport seats, a color-coordinated center console, dashboard, and door panels, a head-up display, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connectivity, a Mark Levinson sound system, ambient lighting, automatic climate control, a heated steering wheel, and a center console plaque that identifies this car as #165 of 550 Inspiration Series models produced.
Photo: Bring a Trailer In terms of electronic driver aids, there's the Pre-Collision System, Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Intuitive Parking Assist, a blind-spot monitor, rear cross traffic alert, and lane-keep assist.
As for that previously-mentioned 5.0-liter V8 engine , it's pushing 471 horsepower and 398 lb-ft (540 Nm) of torque to the rear wheels via a 10-speed automatic gearbox and a Torsen limited-slip rear differential. In a straight line, the LC 500 can get you from zero to 60 mph (97 kph) in just 4.5 seconds. More than quick enough, I'd say.
So, what do you guys think, is $147,000 (plus a buyer's fee) too much for an LC 500? Or is the Inspiration Series totally worth it? Me personally, I can understand the valuation, but I also don't see these going up in value again any time soon. I think I'd just rather have a regular LC 500 Convertible.

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.
Volkswagen ID. Cross prices by trim in the UK
After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.
The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.
Following the ID. Polo , the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.
When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.
Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.
The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.
With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.
All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.
Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.
Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.
The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).
Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.
Volkswagen ID. Cross trim (UK) | On sale in the UK | Price (OTR RPP inc VAT)
ID. Cross Life 37 kWh 135 PS | Expected January 2027 | £26,985 ($35,500)
ID. Cross Life 52 kWh 211 PS | November 19 2026 | £30,260 ($40,000)
ID. Cross Style 37 kWh 135 PS | Expected January 2027 | £30,400 ($40,100)
ID. Cross Style 52 kWh 211 PS | November 19 2026 | £33,675 ($44,500)
Volkswagen ID. Cross prices and expected availability by trim in the UK
In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.
As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”
Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan , which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

source_document.body:
Q3 2026 Freight Earnings: What 74 Companies Told Us
Rates turned, costs bit and capacity kept leaving. Here is what the Q3 2026 freight earnings season says about the market heading into the 2027 bid season .
The short answer
Q3 2026 freight earnings confirmed a supply-driven recovery : SONAR tender rejections (STRI) averaged 14.5%, nearly triple a year ago, while tender volume (STVI) rose 8.5%.
Pricing exposure picked the winners. One-way truckload fleets expanded margins; dedicated and small contract fleets absorbed the cost squeeze.
Diesel was the biggest cost , averaging $5.56 per gallon (+48% y/y), and inflated revenue across every mode.
LTL tonnage turned and accelerated in October, while ocean and forwarding profits likely peaked.
By the numbers
14.5% STRI Q3 average, vs. 5.3% a year ago
$3.46 NTI spot rate per mile, up 50% y/y
$5.56 Diesel per gallon, up 48% y/y
89.2% Knight-Swift TL adjusted OR, 700 bps better
The Q3 2026 freight earnings season is nearly complete. Of the 71 companies on SONAR’s core roster, 66 have reported, along with eight supplemental companies, from truckload carriers and railroads to ocean lines, brokers and freight technology firms. Our full Q3 2026 Freight Earnings Blue Book scores every segment and the largest carriers. This is the short version.
A supply-driven freight market, not a demand boom
The clearest signal in Q3 came from SONAR’s tender data. Carriers rejected 14.5% of contracted loads on average, up from 5.3% a year earlier, while accepted volume grew in the single digits. That combination points to capacity leaving the market, not a flood of new freight.
STRI.USA : tender rejections climbed from about 6% in November 2025 to a peak near 17.6% in late June and stood at 12.87% on Nov. 13, roughly double year-ago levels. Source: SONAR.
STVI.USA : outside holiday dips, tender volume has held between roughly 11,000 and 12,500 all year. Steady volume plus high rejections means tight supply. Source: SONAR.
Carrier commentary matched the data. Knight-Swift, Schneider, Covenant and TFI International all shrank their fleets by 4% to 12% and pushed rate. Roper, parent of DAT, described the load board recovery the same way: driven by supply, not demand.
Truckload: pricing exposure picked the winners
Truckload delivered the season’s sharpest split. Carriers with large one-way networks repriced quickly; fleets tied to dedicated contracts and annual index escalators could not keep up with fuel, wage and insurance costs.
Carrier | One-way rev/truck/week | Dedicated rev/truck/week
Werner | +34.3% | +5.6%
Schneider | +21.4% | +3.1%
Covenant (expedited) | +12.0% | +6.2%
Knight-Swift, with about three-quarters of its truckload revenue in one-way freight, lifted revenue per mile 12.2% while cost per mile rose 3.8%, improving its adjusted truckload operating ratio by 700 basis points to 89.2%. J.B. Hunt’s dedicated segment went the other way, with operating income down 22%. Smaller contract fleets fared worst: Pamt posted a 109.1% truckload operating ratio, its 12th straight truckload loss.
The carriers that could reprice fast won Q3. Everyone else is waiting on the 2027 bid season.
LTL tonnage turned the corner
After two years of declines, LTL volumes turned positive at Old Dominion in September and accelerated across the group in October: ArcBest’s tonnage rose about 15%, Saia’s about 10% and XPO’s about 6.5%. Shipments are getting heavier, which suggests LTL is winning freight that tight truckload capacity no longer moves cheaply. XPO posted the best margin progress, with an adjusted LTL operating ratio of 80.1%, 260 basis points better.
Rail: fuel split the Class I railroads
All six Class I railroads grew revenue 12% to 15% on volume gains of just 3% to 6%. How each absorbed a 56% to 69% jump in fuel expense decided its margins. CSX improved its operating ratio about 420 basis points, while Norfolk Southern’s worsened 280 basis points. Intermodal was the bright spot, with record volume at CSX and a 27% intermodal revenue gain at Union Pacific.
Ocean and forwarding: record profits, softer 2027
Ocean carriers and forwarders posted the biggest profit swings of the season, almost entirely on price. Maersk’s loaded rates rose 46% on slightly lower volume, and Expeditors grew earnings per share 62% as AI-related air freight from hyperscalers and their suppliers surged. Carriers expect 2027 to be softer: Drewry projects container capacity growth of 8.8% against 6.2% demand growth.
What to watch into the 2027 bid season
VCRPM1.USA : van contract rates climbed from about $2.31 per mile a year ago to $2.88, a 12-month high, accelerating in October. Source: SONAR.
Contract rates are still climbing. Knight-Swift expects to open bids with low-to-mid double-digit increases, and Werner expects double-digit gains on the one-way business it reprices in the first half of 2027. Truck orders now trail deliveries ahead of final EPA 2027 rules, so capacity is likely to rebuild slowly. Watch STRI and VCRPM1 through January: if rejections hold above 12%, double-digit contract increases become the base case.
Frequently asked questions
How did freight companies perform in Q3 2026?
Most beat expectations on rising rates, but results split by pricing exposure. One-way truckload fleets such as Knight-Swift expanded margins sharply, while dedicated and small contract fleets absorbed fuel, wage and insurance inflation. Of SONAR’s 71-company core roster, 66 have reported.
Is the 2026 freight recovery driven by demand?
No. SONAR data shows a supply-driven market. Tender rejections (STRI) averaged 14.5% in Q3 versus 5.3% a year earlier, while tender volumes (STVI) rose only 8.5%. Carriers described capacity leaving the market rather than a surge in freight.
How much did truckload rates rise in Q3 2026?
SONAR’s National Truckload Index (NTI) averaged $3.46 per mile in Q3, up about 50% from a year earlier, and van contract rates (VCRPM1) averaged $2.70, up 17.5%. Contract rates reached $2.88 in mid-November ahead of the 2027 bid season.
How did diesel prices affect Q3 freight earnings?
Diesel averaged $5.56 per gallon in Q3, up 48% year over year, and was the most-cited cost headwind. Fuel expense rose 56–69% at the railroads that disclosed it and 64% at FedEx, compressing margins until surcharges caught up.
What should shippers expect in 2027 freight bids?
Carriers are asking for higher contract rates. Knight-Swift expects to open bids with low-to-mid double-digit increases, and Werner expects double-digit increases on the one-way business it reprices in the first half of 2027.
Get the full Q3 2026 Blue Book
The full report covers every segment, company scorecards for the largest truckload, LTL and rail carriers, and the SONAR data behind them. SONAR subscribers can track every index in this article daily, by market.

LeoLabs' new Scout-S fits in a standardized 20-foot container for easy deployment. (Photo: LeoLabs)
WASHINGTON — Space tracking firm LeoLabs today announced it has acquired FishEye Software as it looks to expand its missile defense footprint.
“As a wholly owned subsidiary of LeoLabs, FishEye will strengthen our ability to accelerate delivery of our next-generation radars optimized for missile warning and tracking, such as Scout-X ,” a LeoLabs spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
The highly mobile Scout-X made its debut in June during during US Indo-Pacific Command’s multinational Valiant Shield exercise. The radar fits in a standard shipping container and can detect both satellites and missiles flying at altitudes of about 230 to 1,000 kilometers (143 miles to 621 miles) above the Earth.
Founded in 1997 and headquartered in Massachusetts, FishEye has a pedigree in supporting the Pentagon’s missile defense programs. It is one of several thousand small firms chosen last December for the Missile Defense Agency’s Scalable Homeland Innovative Enterprise Layered Defense ( SHIELD ) contract vehicle, which is worth up to $151 billion through 2035, and supports the Trump administration’s Golden Dome initiative.
“FishEye brings decades of experience developing and integrating software for U.S. missile defense systems,” LeoLabs CEO Tony Frazier said in a statement. “That expertise will help us continue to adapt our proven radar technology for missile warning and tracking, and move those capabilities into operational use quickly.”
While the LeoLabs announcement did not reveal the price tag of the acquisition, FishEye’s revenue is projected to reach approximately $11.9 million this year, according to corporate research website RocketReach.

Boeing's concept for their ORCA Extra-Large Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV)
WASHINGTON — The Navy is getting closer to operationally using several unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) — specifically the Orca, with the service set to receive its third “soon,” according to the commander of Submarine Forces for the US Pacific Fleet.
Additionally, the Navy is making progress on the Combat Autonomous Maritime Platform (CAMP) XLUUV, which is the Navy and the Department of Innovation Unit’s initiative to quickly prototype and field XLUUVs, as well as the Dragonfish large displacement UUV (LDUUV), which replaced the Navy’s nixed Snakehead LDUUV program.
“Those are all progressing toward meaningful operational employment,” Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh said Thursday. “Those systems complement our crewed platforms, expand our reach, increase our operational flexibility, and allow us to accept risks that we wouldn’t take with manned submarines.”
The Orca program is the Navy’s first XLUUV initiative , launched in 2017, and aimed at laying undersea mines. The first test vehicle was delivered in 2023 and the first prototype vehicle was delivered in 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office . The vessel has a range of up to 6,500 nautical miles to support “monthslong, long-range missions” and can accommodate a host of mission payloads, according to Boeing, which makes the vehicle.
Capt. Michael Linn, the program manager for the Undersea Warfare Program Management Office, said that the service is nearing the end of production plans for Orca, and that two of the three prototype vessels have already been delivered. Ultimately, the program will lay the groundwork for other UUV programs like CAMP, he said.
“We’re going to get our third one delivered soon, and that is going to wrap up a long and arduous process of getting Orca over the finish line,” Linn said on Friday. “Once we get it in our hands, we’re going to continue to characterize it. We’re going to put it through its paces and figure out what it really does well and what it doesn’t do well. But the point is I’m fully intent on getting it employed and characterized. CAMP, we’re going to build on what we learned from Orca.”

As Novo awaits an FDA decision for its next-gen obesity asset, the company has presented more data at ObesityWeek that could help buoy sentiment on the amylin/GLP-1 combination that disappointed investors a couple of years ago.
Novo has linked lower doses of next-generation obesity drug candidate CagriSema to more than 20% weight loss in a Phase 3 trial, leading analysts to hail the “strong efficacy.”
Previously, the Danish drugmaker reported 22.7% weight loss in patients who received up to 2.4 mg of the amylin analog cagrilintide and the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide, which combine to make CagriSema, at 68 weeks in the REDEFINE 1 trial. The data disappointed investors, sending Novo’s stock down 20%, and hopes for CagriSema took another hit when it failed to beat Eli Lilly’s Zepbound in February. Yet Novo has continued to position CagriSema as its next-generation weight loss therapy.
The low-dose trial forms part of the positioning push. Novo tested 1-mg and 1.7-mg doses of the cagrilintide and semaglutide combo in REDEFINE 9, sharing the low-dose data Saturday at ObesityWeek 2026 in Washington, D.C. At week 68, patients receiving 1 mg and 1.7 mg weekly doses lost 21% and 20.7% of their body weight, respectively. Patients receiving placebo lost 2% of their body weight. The primary endpoint results, which were statistically significant, reflect the effect had all participants adhered to treatment, Novo said.
The magnitude of effect is “interesting, supporting meaningful efficacy below the highest dose studied in the program,” BMO Capital Markets analysts said in a note to investors. The analysts called the efficacy data “strong,” adding that the study showed “lower doses of CagriSema still deliver substantial weight loss.”
Weight loss “remained strong” in an analysis that assessed the effect regardless of discontinuation or use of weight management rescue intervention, the analysts said. In that assessment, weight loss was 18.6% and 19.4% in the 1 mg and 1.7 mg arms, respectively.

Novo Nordisk executives set a high bar for itself when it projected CagriSema could achieve 25% weight loss. When the GLP-1 combo didn’t hit that mark, investors reeled.
December 20, 2024

The results appear similar to the weight loss seen in REDEFINE 1 , the analysts said. REDEFINE 1 allowed flexible dosing, and only 57% of patients were on the 2.4 mg dose at week 68. The proportion of patients on lower doses means it is possible that REDEFINE 1 “did not capture the full weight loss profile of CagriSema,” the analysts said. Novo is running the 80-week Phase 3 REDEFINE 11 trial to explore further weight loss.
Tolerability looks similar across REDEFINE 1 and REDEFINE 9, the analysts said. Novo reported nausea and vomiting rates of 55% and 26%, respectively, in REDEFINE 1. Despite receiving lower doses, 62% and 27% of patients in the 1 mg arm of REDEFINE 9 had nausea and vomiting, respectively. Nausea and vomiting rates were 66% and 32%, respectively, in the 1.7 mg arm.
The REDEFINE 9 results formed the basis of one of five CagriSema presentations at ObesityWeek. Novo also used the event to share posthoc REDEFINE 1 analyses showing that 67.8% of adults on the 2.4 mg dose lost at least 5% of their body weight by week eight and that 73.1% reported a meaningful improvement in physical function at week 68. The data add to Novo’s evidence as it prepares to launch CagriSema, which is currently under review at the FDA with a decision expected by the end of the year.
“With U.S. approval decision for obesity expected in 4Q26 management sees an opportunity to build on the physician familiarity and wealth of clinical data the company has established for semaglutide,” the analysts said. “Amylin brings a compelling new mechanism to market with differentiated benefits vs. existing therapies.”

It is 9:40 p.m. in a regional hub. A late inbound flight has squeezed the connection window for LD-3 containers bound for three cities. Nobody has noticed yet. By morning, the retailer will, and so will its customers.
In air cargo, this is how most service problems begin: quietly, hours before anyone picks up a phone. And it is why a growing number of carriers are rethinking what customer service means. The best support call, they argue, is the one that never has to happen. Artificial intelligence is what is finally making that possible.
The problem with waiting for the phone to ring
For decades, cargo customer service has been reactive by design. A shipper notices a package hasn’t moved, calls or emails the airline, and an agent starts digging through booking records, flight status and warehouse scans. By the time an answer comes back, the delay is history and the only thing left to manage is disappointment.
That model was tolerable when air cargo meant heavy freight moving on forgiving timelines. It does not hold up in domestic e-commerce, where shoppers expect next-day delivery and retailers measure carriers by the hour. A missed connection that once cost a day now costs a customer.
The cost lands inside the airline too. Every “where is my shipment?” inquiry ties up an agent who could be solving a real problem. Service teams spend their days explaining what already went wrong instead of preventing what is about to.
From tracking to predicting
Tracking tells you where a shipment is. Prediction tells you where it is going to be, and whether that is a problem.
The raw material has existed for years: booking data, flight schedules, load factors, acceptance and handling scans, weather feeds, historical transit times. What has changed is the ability to read all of it at once, continuously, and spot the patterns that come before a failure. A tight connection on a route that runs late every Friday. A station that slows down when volume spikes. A flight trending toward a weight restriction that will bump cargo.
AI models are well suited to this kind of work. They do not get tired at the end of a shift, and they do not wait for a customer to complain before looking. They flag the shipment at risk while there is still time to act on it.
That shift only works on modern infrastructure. Cloud-native platforms such as SmartKargo track every shipment from booking to delivery, giving AI a complete, real-time picture rather than fragments stitched together from legacy systems. Visibility is the foundation. Prediction is what you build on top of it, and it is the job SmartKargo’s AINOC was built to do.
What proactive service looks like
Go back to that hub at 9:40 p.m. In a predictive operation, the system flags the 300 parcels the moment the inbound flight slips. It checks the next departures with available belly space and proposes a rebooking. The ops team approves it in minutes.
Then the service side kicks in. The retailer gets a message before it has a reason to ask: two shipments rerouted, new arrival times attached, delivery promises intact. No inquiry is logged. No agent spends an hour reconstructing a timeline. For the end customer, nothing happened at all.
AI is changing how that message gets written, too. When a shipment is flagged, the system drafts the outreach for the agent: a recommended email to the retailer’s operations team listing the affected shipments, the cause, the new arrival times and the recovery plan, and a short text for the consignee waiting at the other end. Each draft fits its audience. The shipper gets detail it can act on. The person expecting the package gets two sentences and a new delivery window.
The agent reviews, adjusts and sends in seconds instead of composing from scratch in the middle of a disruption. Routine updates, such as a confirmed reroute, can go out automatically. Sensitive ones, such as a missed delivery promise for a major account, stay with a person. Either way, the customer hears from the airline first, in plain language, before frustration has a chance to build.
That is the quiet payoff of prediction. Some problems are fixed outright. Others cannot be avoided, but the customer hears about them first, with a plan already in place. Shippers rarely forgive surprises. They often forgive delays they were warned about, especially when the carrier has already acted.
People still make the call
None of this removes people from the picture. It changes what they do. When AI handles the routine monitoring and the first alert, service agents and ops controllers can focus on the judgment calls: which shipment gets the last space on the evening flight, how to handle a high-value customer, when to escalate.
The technology has limits, and carriers that adopt it well are honest about them. A prediction is a probability, not a promise. Models are only as good as the data feeding them, which is why clean, end-to-end shipment data matters more than any single algorithm. And the alert is worthless if no one is empowered to act on it.
The new measure of service
For years, cargo service was judged by how fast an agent answered and how well they explained a delay. That yardstick is changing. The carriers pulling ahead in e-commerce are measured by how few problems their customers ever see.
It is a higher bar, and a more honest one. Shippers do not want great apologies. They want packages that arrive when promised, and a partner who calls them before they have to call in. With AI watching every shipment, every hour, that standard is no longer aspirational. It is becoming the cost of doing business in the skies.
About SmartKargo
SmartKargo is the cloud-based logistics platform connecting airlines to the e-commerce economy. By automating shipments end-to-end and turning passenger flights into cargo revenue, SmartKargo helps airlines launch new products in weeks and gives shippers faster, more reliable delivery than ground networks can offer.

Savannah/Hilton Head International Airport opened a 36-acre air cargo complex last week, adding two freight buildings and space for more cargo carriers. The Savannah Area Chamber of Commerce put the cost at about $80 million, including a taxiway extension and a new bridge over Gulfstream Road.
What’s Related
The complex sits at the north end of the airport and has direct access to the runway and the apron, where planes park to load and unload. It can accommodate wide-body aircraft such as the Boeing 767-300 and Airbus A300-600. The site also has cold storage infrastructure, and the airport is marketing space to freight forwarders, cargo airlines and companies that handle temperature-sensitive shipments .
FedEx and UPS signed on early
The larger cargo building spans about 65,000 square feet and was designed for a single tenant, with space for sorting packages, offices, and customer service. The airport said in its 2024 annual report that FedEx had committed to the single-tenant building and UPS had signed for 15,000 square feet in the other building, which was designed for multiple carriers.
At the opening, the airport listed three units available for lease, totaling 45,000 square feet. The largest is 25,000 square feet, and the other two are 10,000 square feet each. The units have truck docks on one side and access to the aircraft apron on the other, giving tenants a direct route for moving freight between trucks and planes.
Planes can enter and leave at the same time
The airport extended Taxiway G and built a bridge over Gulfstream Road so one aircraft can enter the cargo area while another leaves. The work added about 13,500 square yards of taxiway pavement, along with lighting, signs, pavement markings, and drainage.
The project took about five years from the first discussions through construction, Savannah Airport Commission Executive Director Greg Kelly told WJCL. Kelly told WTOC that grants covered about $10 million of the project and that the airport paid for the buildings out of its own budget.
Close to port and two highways
The airport sits along Interstate 95 and less than 10 miles from Interstate 16, which gives trucks a route west toward Atlanta. The cargo complex is also minutes from the Port of Savannah and two major rail lines, putting it near the region’s other freight connections.
The airport handled 1,236 tons of cargo in October, up about 12% from the same month a year earlier. Through the first 10 months of 2026, however, it handled about 10,400 tons, roughly even with the same period in 2025.

Eli Lilly’s business development team has inked 14 buyouts this year so far, with Calytrix Bio tucking into the pharma’s oncology pipeline.
Eli Lilly is making good on a promise to buy more biotechs. The GLP-1 juggernaut has offered up to $1.5 billion in cash for privately held Calytrix Bio, which focuses on chronic blood cancers.
The deal includes an upfront payment and additional milestone-based payments offered for certain clinical and regulatory events. Exact financial terms were not provided in a Monday morning release .
Calytrix’s lead asset is a biparatopic antibody for mutant calreticulin-driven essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis, both chronic blood cancers known as myeloproliferative neoplasms. This candidate, which was not named, is meant to be disease-modifying with a safety profile that can allow for early and long-term treatment.
Treatment for patients with these cancers typically involves managing symptoms and complications, rather than addressing the underlying disease like in other cancers, Calytrix explained.

The buy will fit into Lilly’s massive oncology portfolio, which helped the pharma reach 100% growth for key products during the third quarter. During a October earnings report , Lilly’s executives pledged to ink more buyouts to further bolster its entire pipeline. Jacob Van Naarden, president of oncology and head of corporate business development, even hinted at some riskier, early-stage bets.
“Risk is really our friend here. Risk allows us to actually create value,” Van Naarden said. He also said the company has conducted several deals with small, privately held companies that were not disclosed.
Calytrix seems to meet that early-stage bar. The company launched in 2025 out of J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital, the life sciences venture capital arm of global investment manager J.P. Morgan Asset Management, according to the release. The company has conducted a series A led by the firm plus a series B with Avoro Ventures. Financial details of the rounds were not disclosed.
The Calytrix acquisition marks Lilly’s 14th disclosed transaction of the year. Most recently, Lilly picked up autoimmune-focused Merida Biosciences for just under $2.9 billion in cash at the end of August . Lilly’s largest deal so far came in March, when it bought Centessa Pharmaceuticals for $8.14 billion.
