Containerized imports through U.S ports reached a record 2.67 million twenty foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, pushing volumes above the previous peak set during the pandemic-era surge.
Rising shipments from China and a rebound at East and Gulf Coast ports fueled the record, according to Descartes data.
Imports totaled 2,674,808 TEUs, up 5% from September and 16% from October 2025. The total exceeded the previous monthly record of 2,622,465 TEUs, set in May 2022, by 2%.
The increase lifted imports for the first 10 months of 2026 to 2.3% above the same period a year earlier. October marked the second consecutive month in which cumulative imports ran ahead of 2025, following eight months below the prior year’s pace.
Imports from China rose for a fourth consecutive month, reaching 987,805 TEUs, and the highest monthly total since January 2025. Volumes increased 6.9% from September and 22.9% from a year earlier, accounting for approximately half of the overall U.S. monthly gain.
China’s share of U.S. container imports increased to 36.9%, from 36.3% in September. Plastics, furniture and bedding, and toys, games and sporting goods were the largest categories by volume.
Growth extended beyond China as imports from the top 10 countries of origin increased 5.8% from September, with seven posting gains. South Korea and Germany each recorded monthly increases of 22.8%, while Vietnam, Taiwan and India declined. All 10 origins recorded higher volumes than in October 2025.
East and Gulf Coast ports gain ground
Houston recorded the largest monthly volume increase among the top 10 U.S. ports, adding 42,665 TEUs, a gain of 26.7%. Savannah imports rose 12.6%, Norfolk increased 17.7%, and Charleston’s climbed 18.6%. By contrast, volumes fell 1.4% at Los Angeles, 2% at Long Beach and 10.9% at Oakland.
The gains shifted a larger share of imports toward East and Gulf Coast gateways. The five leading ports in those regions handled 39.9% of U.S. container imports, up from 36.7% in September. The five leading West Coast gateways’ share fell to 44.9%, from 47%.
Across the Gulf Coast, imports increased 24% to 266,905 TEUs, the highest monthly total since Descartes began tracking the regional measure in August 2023. Houston accounted for approximately 83% of the region’s net monthly increase.
Descartes cautioned that the sharp gains partly reflected a recovery from September’s weaker volumes. Combined imports at Houston, Savannah, Norfolk and Charleston rose 18.1% month over month but were only 3.6% above August levels. Extended peak-season demand and uneven vessel arrival timing may also have contributed, the report said.
Transit delays build alongside higher volumes
The record month followed a sustained period of elevated imports, with monthly volumes exceeding 2.5 million TEUs since July. Meanwhile, the unweighted average transit delay across 10 tracked gateways increased to 6.3 days in October, from six days in September and 4.2 days in June.
Seven of the 10 gateways recorded higher delays in October. Descartes said the gradual increase could indicate that sustained import volumes were putting pressure on the inland logistics network, although November’s data would help establish whether that pressure was intensifying.
The report’s transit-delay measure compares the estimated arrival date initially declared on a bill of lading with the date Descartes receives the corresponding U.S. Customs and Border Protection-processed data. The underlying import figures use an initial compilation of customs bill-of-lading records and may be revised.
Policy and routing risks remain
Beyond port performance, Descartes flagged changing maritime fees, canal availability and security conditions as planning risks. The Trump administration suspended port fees on Chinese ships through January 9, 2027, while increased Panama Canal transit availability and selected returns to Suez Canal routings were changing options on some services. Services through the Suez remained dependent on regional security conditions, the report noted.
Closer to home, the report indicated concerns over ongoing contract talks with watchmen at Los Angeles and Long Beach represented by the International Longshore and Warehouse Union , with the contract extended through November 20. Employers warned that a potential strike could affect terminals handling more than half of the two ports’ combined cargo.
Why it matters: October’s record shows import volumes reaching new highs despite year-to-date growth that remains modest, with resulting pressure distributed unevenly across ports.

Acura Recalls ZDX Electric Crossover for Potential Loss of Brake Pressure
7 photos
Photo: Acura
A zero-emission crossover with GM underpinnings, the Acura ZDX was discontinued after the 2025 model year due to pitiful demand in the US market, a problem exacerbated by expiring federal incentives. Even though it's no longer produced, the Acura-branded model has been hit with a recall that affects all-wheel-drive specifications delivered for MY24 in the US market.
26V7350 is what the safety boffins at the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration call this campaign, which comprises 14,648 vehicles. The safety concern here stems from the electric brake control module. According to American Honda Motor, the EBCM software can miscalculate the vehicle's reference speed.
When this happens, the subject module may command an inappropriate reduction in brake pressure, compromising the braking performance of the affected vehicles. The miscalculation apparently occurs in very specific conditions. To the point, when any sort of wheel slip and light braking occur together with driving over a disturbance in the road.
American Honda Motor also notes a brake pedal that is either released or reapplied in the process. On high-friction surfaces, the iffy software interprets the resulting data as evidence of excessive slip. This, in turn, prompts the subject module to reduce brake pressure, reducing brake capability without any warning.
General Motors is identified in the recall documentation as the manufacturer of the suspect vehicles and the supplier of the brake control module software, which is split between no fewer than nine part numbers by American Honda Motor. Suspect production dates range from December 19, 2023, through January 22, 2025.
Photo: Acura Spring Hill, Tennessee, served as the home of the ZDX, whose BEV3 platform is shared with the Cadillac Lyriq, Honda Prologue, and Chevrolet Blazer EV . Rear-wheel drive by nature yet all-wheel drive by choice, the ZDX was never a big seller in the United States market. Only 109 units were delivered so far this year, 12,005 in 2025, and 7,391 in 2024, making it a bit of a commercial blunder.
As noted earlier, only dual-motor vehicles feature the suspect EBCM software. Honda first determined that such a defect exists in August 2024, resulting in recall 24V614. More than two years later, General Motors supplied additional information that forced the Japanese automaker to recall the ZDX yet again.
Thankfully for both customers and American Honda Motor's legal department, no injuries potentially associated with the described condition have been reported thus far. Even so, a temporary reduction in braking pressure is nothing to scoff at when the subject vehicle weighs 5,904 pounds (2,678 kilograms) at the very least. The performance-oriented Type S is listed with 6,052 lbs (2,745 kgs).
Customers who have accepted OTA terms and conditions will receive the updated EBCM software over the air. Everyone else can arrange a free-of-charge update at the Acura dealership of their liking. The new software package includes a revised calibration that corrects the false wheel slippage detection condition.
Customers will be notified by first-class mail no later than December 14, 2026. In the meantime, customers may check if their ZDXs need the update by running the 17-character VIN on the NHTSA's website.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 16, 2026
A push by Indonesia to capture at least 70% of the benefits from mining permits sent local mining shares lower Monday, as President Prabowo Subianto raised the prospect of greater state ownership without explaining how the proposed share would be calculated. Prabowo instructed ministers to increase the state’s share of mining returns during a speech Saturday in Palu, Central Sulawesi, news agencies including Reuters and Bloomberg reported. His office described the target as a share of proceeds from managing mining permits, leaving the treatment of existing operations unspecified. “From now on, all mining permits, at least 70% must benefit the state,” Prabowo said in Indonesian. “If necessary, the shares should be state-controlled.” The intervention could affect investment decisions in the world’s dominant nickel producer and a major copper supplier. Indonesia mined an estimated 2.6 million tonnes of nickel last year, about two-thirds of global output, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Amman Mineral Internasional (IDX: AMMN) shares dropped 3.5% and Merdeka Copper Gold (IDX: MDKA) fell 4.8% in Monday trading. That compared with a 1.1% decline in the Jakarta Composite Index, Dow Jones reported.
No timetable
The remarks marked an escalation in Indonesia’s rhetoric on state control, BMO Capital Markets commodities analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel said in a Monday note.
The presidency’s account didn’t define whether the 70% would be measured against revenue, profit or another measure of economic benefit. It also gave no implementation timetable. The statement therefore leaves investors without a formula for assessing the financial impact on individual mines. A separate proposal earlier this year envisaged allocating 70% of mineral and coal output to the government and 30% to operators under a gross-split arrangement. Energy Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said in June that the plan had been dropped after consultation with Prabowo, BMO noted. Prabowo also called for exports to pass through a designated agency to prevent companies understating shipment volumes. His office presented the measure as a way to improve oversight of natural-resource earnings.
Existing stakes
Indonesia already holds a 51% interest in PT Freeport Indonesia, the operator of the Grasberg copper-gold complex. Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) owns the remaining 49%. The government has separately outlined plans to raise its Freeport Indonesia stake to 63% by 2041 in connection with extending the operation’s contract. That timetable, described by Lahadalia in February, illustrates how changes in state ownership can be tied to specific operating agreements. Saturday’s broader demand leaves a different question for miners: how the government would count taxes, royalties, dividends and ownership towards its proposed share, and whether existing agreements would be protected.

As Europe’s defense ministries look to limit dependency on American technology and major software company Palantir Technologies for critical military functions, a growing number of firms within the region are competing for their business.
Last week, Germany’s Helsing unveiled military intelligence software called Clarity. It is part of a broader market for AI-powered systems designed to accelerate military decision-making by helping sift through vast quantities of data to identify threats and recommend action, including targeting and attacks.
But Europe currently lacks an exact equivalent that matches Palantir’s scale, deployment footprint and operational experience, some government and military officials say.
That gives European militaries a dilemma: pursue homegrown systems that promise greater autonomy but may be less mature, or rely on a proven platform despite concerns about long-term strategic dependence.
The Trump administration has pushed Europe to take on much greater responsibility for its own security as Washington scales back its military presence in the region, and has placed pressure on the transatlantic NATO alliance.
European officials face similar trade-offs between autonomy and capability across a range of military capabilities, including in the area of satellite communications, which is dominated by Elon Musk’s US company SpaceX.
Ukraine last week reported further significant disruptions of its access to SpaceX, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
France, a vocal advocate for European autonomy, is developing a sovereign AI-enabled military platform called Arcadia. Alexandre Lahousse, the deputy head of France’s defense procurement agency, told Reuters it would include multiple suppliers. The agency plans to award at least some contracts by year’s end and to have an operational version available for field deployment by mid-2027, he said.
Germany, which is also aiming to deploy an AI-based military data integration platform from next year, is weighing domestic and other European options.
It has narrowed down a shortlist to a handful of solutions, which does not include Palantir, a person familiar with the matter said. The person said the solutions under consideration would not match Palantir’s capabilities but would be good enough, ensure national data sovereignty and should be able to achieve about 80% of what is needed within a year.
The Netherlands currently uses some Palantir software but says it wants a European alternative within two years. The Dutch military is meeting potential suppliers and will likely require a combination of Dutch and other European providers, Dutch arms procurement minister Derk Boswijk told Reuters.
“We have a lot of knowledge in Europe when it comes to AI and decision-making. But it’s very fragmented, and that is the problem,” Boswijk said.
U.S. Army Maj. Steven McPherson trains on the Maven Smart System, Feb. 20, 2026. (Master Sgt. Whitney Hughes/U.S. Army Photo)
Palantir’s Maven Smart System has been widely used by Ukraine in its fight against Russia while the Pentagon has adopted it as its core military software and has used it in its war with Iran this year.
“I’ve yet to find anything that can pull together as much of a diverse set of data and allow us the ability to make sense of that data as flexibly,” NATO’s top commander, US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, told Reuters this summer.
NATO’s military headquarters adopted Palantir’s Maven Smart System last year and said in June that it was ready for routine alliance-wide operational use.
Militaries are wrestling with many questions, including around data security, who trains the AI systems, and ensuring different platforms work seamlessly together, said Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, Germany’s army chief, at a conference in Berlin on Friday.
“There’s the issue of interoperability when we fight in alliances — and we always fight in alliances.”
NATO officials have previously warned of an increased threat from Russia, which they say could potentially mount ​a large-scale assault on allied territory as early as 2029. Moscow denies aggressive intentions.
Helsing said it could supply an initial version of its Clarity software within a matter of months to the German military’s Lithuania brigade, widely viewed as the Bundeswehr unit most likely to see frontline combat in the event of a conflict with Russia.
Other European makers of military software include Denmark’s Systematic, whose SitaWare product is used by the Bundeswehr and parts of NATO, as well as traditional defense companies like France’s Thales and Safran, plus startups such as Paris-based Comand AI.
For its part, Palantir has sought to reassure Europeans that its military AI system used by NATO has no “kill ‌switch.” Palantir’s international chief Louis Mosley told Reuters there remains demand in Europe for its products including in the UK, where the defense ministry last year signed a three-year enterprise agreement with the US company.
Mosley added he still hopes to persuade Germany to adopt Palantir’s software with the pitch that it has battlefield-tested capability that works today.

Companies at BIO-Europe said shifting U.S. politics have created an opening to promote Canada’s strengths to European partners.
U.S. political uncertainty has pushed Canadian service providers and biotechs to seek new business opportunities in Europe, firms told BioSpace at the recent BIO-Europe conference in Cologne, Germany.
Although Canada has long-standing U.S. ties, Europe is increasingly perceived as a more stable continent to engage markets. Canada also has expedient regulatory and economic advantages. The country has flown under the radar more than its southern neighbor, making the present a good time to represent its advantages.
More than 110 companies attended BIO-Europe, wrote Silke Ditgen, trade commissioner for the Consulate of Canada, based in Germany, in an email.
“The growing ties between Canada and Europe are certainly a contributing factor, and there is strong momentum at the moment,” wrote Jeannine Burkhard, head of public affairs and stakeholder relations at BioQuébec, in an email.
Canada and the European Union announced an “Alliance for the Future” at a two-day summit in October.
BIO-Europe is Europe’s largest and longest-running international partnering conference for the biotechnology, biopharma and life sciences industries.
Strong Canadian presence
Although the Canadian life science scene is very much connected to the U.S., particularly in hubs such as Boston and San Diego, there is more effort to expand the network outside of America, Burkhard wrote.
U.S. instability has pushed Montréal-based CRO Vantage BioTrials to increasingly look to European biotechs, said company President Vatche Bartekian.
Caroline Dubic, director of business development at CRO/CDMO Royalmount BioPharma in Montréal, agreed, adding the uncertainty at the FDA and the National Institutes of Health makes Canada an increasingly attractive option to conduct business and engage in partnerships.
On BIO-Europe’s opening day, November 9, Bioscience Association Manitoba (BAM), BIOQuébec and BioWin, the health innovation cluster of Wallonia, Belgium, announced a trilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MOU).
“Through this new agreement, the three organizations aim to connect the complementary strengths of Québec, Manitoba and Wallonia, facilitating business development, knowledge exchange and international partnerships,” the press release stated.
As for Canadian biotechs that attended BIO-Europe, they are seeking licensing deals, co-development partners, clinical collaborators and acquisition opportunities, Ditgen wrote. Europe hosts many global pharmaceutical leaders including Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Roche, Novartis, Sanofi, Merck KGaA and Novo Nordisk.
“Events such as BIO-Europe have become major partnering venues where Canadian companies can meet dozens of potential partners in a few days,” Ditgen wrote. “For many early-stage biotech firms, a licensing agreement with a European pharmaceutical company may be more valuable than launching independently in the U.S.”
The advantages of going Canadian
Canada has an efficient clinical trial ecosystem to conduct trials, with numerous CROs and organizations to facilitate studies, Burkhard wrote. There is also high-quality research, access to diverse and treatment-naïve patient populations and strength in emerging technologies like AI-driven drug discovery, precision medicine, cell and gene therapies, biomanufacturing and regenerative medicine, Ditgen wrote.
Advantages of working in Canada include Health Canada reviewing clinical trial applications within 30 days upon receipt of a complete application; its alignment with the FDA, European Medicines Agency and Swissmedic for multisite clinical trials and funding programs and tax incentives for clinical research, Dubic explained.
In the past, potential European clients expressed reluctance on working with Canada due to time zone differences, Dubic added. However, she noted that clients are now discovering an upside: work gets done overnight and is waiting in their inboxes by morning.
As Montréal is in the Eastern Time zone, this is also attractive for Europeans for communications, she said, as well as having bilingual French language ability.
Most of Canada’s 1,000-plus biotechs are headquartered in and around the three major hubs of Montréal in Quebec, Toronto in Ontario, and Vancouver in British Columbia, with another growing cluster in the Calgary‒Edmonton Corridor in Alberta.
Canadian R&D hasn’t been as historically strong as in the U.S. and Europe, said SpeciLife Founder and President Katia Dahan, based in Montréal. But with the burgeoning interest in Europe, the time is ripe for Canadians to more boldly champion its life sciences strengths on the global stage, added Kimberly Hu, business development and strategic account manager.

China Revolutionizes Car Theft, With a BYD EV Stolen Right in Front of the Customer During Delivery
6 photos
Photo: Autohome
We've already known that whatever the Western companies do, Chinese companies do faster and cheaper. Unfortunately, this is also true for car theft, with a BYD Song EV stolen right in front of its future owner during the delivery process. At the time, the car was supposed to get its windows tinted, but the car just vanished from the lot.
Due to modern vehicles featuring advanced car-theft protection, car thieves are among the most resourceful in the business. They have to master high-tech methods to defeat anti-theft measures that carmakers integrate into their vehicles. However, most of the time, social engineering still works pretty well. A recent case in China shows that local thieves might be ahead of their peers from Western countries.
The buyer of a BYD Song EV saw their car stolen right in front of them, while awaiting delivery at the dealership. Worse, the future owner was an older man who was gifted the car to celebrate his 60th birthday. Instead of the festive moment he thought it would be, the moment turned into an adventure to secure the car after it was stolen during the delivery process.
Specifically, the customer requested the dealership to tint the windows before delivery. His family had paid 155,000 yuan ($21,500) in full for the car. They had just completed the paperwork, including invoicing and the temporary registration and license plate. Around 6 PM, while they were waiting in the customer lounge for the car to be washed and fitted with window film, a salesperson informed them that the vehicle had disappeared.
What looked like a perfectly normal celebratory moment turned into a full-time adventure as the family and dealership staff tried to locate and seize the stolen vehicle. After a chase that lasted more than an hour and covered over 20 km, they managed to intercept the car. The police took the driver into custody shortly afterward, putting an end to the drama.
While thieves stealing cars from dealerships are nothing new , this one used an ingenious method to do it in the middle of the day, without raising concerns. The suspect was dressed as a BYD employee at the time of his arrest. This made everyone suspicious that it was an inside job. However, upon closer inspection, the uniform did not quite match those worn by actual staff at the dealership.
The investigation revealed that the thief had never been an employee of a BYD dealership, and he bought the BYD-branded uniform online. The suspect had a prior record of car theft , and he was apparently "mentally unstable." However, questions still remain about security lapses at the BYD dealership that allowed the thief to steal the car during the delivery process.
In the aftermath of the event , the family declined to take delivery of the previously stolen vehicle. They have also requested punitive "triple damages" under Chinese customer protection laws. However, the dealership rejected the demand, arguing that they were also victims of the theft. Instead, they agreed to refund the full payment of the car and the insurance policy. The dealership also reimbursed the family for the round-trip travel and lodging expenses.

Members of the family behind the collapsed R&R Family of Companies are listed as executives of a newly established Pittsburgh-area logistics business, even as former R&R chief executive Richard Stephen Francis navigates personal Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in Florida.
Pennsylvania Department of State records show Giant Logistics LLC was organized on Nov. 13, 2025, with an effective date of Jan. 1, 2026.
R&R’s operations began shutting down in January, leaving hundreds of employees without jobs and carriers and other freight-related businesses pursuing unpaid invoices .
The company’s organizer was listed as Richard J. Francis, the youngest son of R&R founder Rich Francis.
A Sept. 29 annual report identifies Jonathan Francis as Giant Logistics’ president, with Richard Francis and Clint Prosperi listed as vice presidents. All three are also identified as company governors.
Jonathan R. Francis, Rich Francis’ oldest son, previously served as vice president of R&R Express’ Company Assets Division, according to his professional profile. Prosperi, another former R&R executive, is also a member of the Francis family by marriage.
The corporate filings establish an overlap between individuals associated with R&R and Giant Logistics, but do not establish whether the new business acquired R&R assets, customers or freight contracts.
In a Nov. 13 email to FreightWaves, Rich Francis said Richard J. Francis was his son and there was no connection between the two companies.
“I have no ownership in Giant Logistics. There is no connection between R & R and Giant,” Francis wrote.
The elder Francis’ personal bankruptcy disclosures, however, identify Giant Logistics as a source of employment income. His filings reported approximately $37,078 in monthly income from commissioned sales work at the company.
The disclosures do not establish that Francis holds an ownership interest in Giant Logistics.
Bankruptcy creditor seeks financial records
Francis filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Sept. 22 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Middle District of Florida.
His bankruptcy schedules reported approximately $12.67 million in assets and $7.46 million in liabilities, including an approximately $8.5 million residence in Marco Island, Florida.
The proceedings have drawn attention from creditors, including Varilease Finance Inc., which is listed in the bankruptcy’s largest unsecured creditors filing with a $10.68 million claim arising from a personal guarantee.
On Nov. 3, Varilease filed a notice seeking testimony and financial records from Francis as part of the bankruptcy proceedings.
The examination is scheduled for Dec. 10, with requested documents due Dec. 3. The creditor’s requests include information about Francis’ employment and compensation arrangements, financial transactions, property holdings and other assets.
The requests are part of the bankruptcy discovery process and do not constitute findings of wrongdoing.
The court also approved the employment of Seese, P.A., as counsel for Francis in his capacity as debtor-in-possession on Nov. 10.
Francis’ initial meeting of creditors was held and concluded Oct. 27. The U.S. trustee has indicated that no official committee of creditors will be appointed until further notice.
The bankruptcy docket lists Jan. 20, 2027, as the original deadline for filing a Chapter 11 reorganization plan and disclosure statement. An Oct. 21 hearing memorandum called for a Dec. 21, 2026, deadline, although the memorandum itself states that it is not an official court order.
Why it matters: The emergence of another Francis-linked freight business raises questions about what became of R&R’s personnel and operations following its collapse.

NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — In early November, Taiwan’s National Security Council secretary-general tracked more than 100 Chinese military-linked vessels near his island.
But given its scale, the massive flotilla that included coast guard vessels alongside navy warships may have had Taiwan’s maritime neighbor Japan in its sights, military experts say.
They say China has sent an outsized number of its far-seas naval deployments to near Japan’s southernmost islands and nearby waters since a political dispute that erupted in November 2025 over a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Takaichi told a Japanese House of Representatives committee session that month that a Chinese naval blockade or armed conflict involving Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for her own country not far away. China claims self-ruled Taiwan as its own and has not ruled out the use of force to take it.
“There is a direct link between Takaichi’s statement and the quality and quantity of deployments,” said Stephen Nagy, a visiting fellow with the Japan Institute for International Affairs think tank in Tokyo. “(China) is also sending a signal to Tokyo that if it continues its current position vis-a-vis Taiwan that Beijing will continue these activities.”
China is using the deployments, including live-fire drills, uncrewed drone missions and voyages by entire aircraft carrier groups, to exert an unrelenting, long-term pressure on Japan without violating international maritime laws, analysts said.
“By repeatedly transiting waters around the (southwestern) Islands, China is gradually normalizing PLA Navy activity within the first island chain, expanding its operational experience and creating a pattern of accepted presence,” said Katsuya Yamamoto, director of the Tokyo-based Sasakawa Peace Foundation’s strategy and deterrence program.
The first island chain includes Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines.
“In other words, it is establishing facts on the ground, or rather at sea, that broaden its future freedom of action,” Yamamoto said.
In the seven weeks after Takaichi’s comment, the U.S. think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies logged a spike in “notable” PLA escalatory moves. Over 2025 overall, it said, China showed just a “slight increase” in the number of PLA naval vessels reported operating in waters around Japan, including an increase in the number of Chinese ships within the contiguous zone of the disputed Senkaku Islands, which China calls the Diaoyu.
Deployments near the uninhabited, Japanese-controlled Senkakus have “remained at very high levels” over the past year as before, while joint Sino-Russian missions around Japan and Chinese naval activity near the outlying Japanese islets around the Miyako Island “seem to have increased”, said Jeffrey Kingston, a professor specializing in Asian studies and history at Temple University, Japan Campus.
Chinese and Russian aircraft patrolled in June over the Sea of Japan, followed by a joint naval passage in July in the Miyako Strait near outlying Japanese islets. Chinese and Russian surveillance aircraft did five separate flights near Japan in October.
Spokespeople for the Chinese ministries of foreign affairs and national defense have called China’s military actions fair, valid and peaceful.
China is probably using military moves as one in a series of measures – some economic – to get back at Takaichi for her November 2025 remarks, Kingston said. “They haven’t forgotten, that’s for sure,” he said. “They are in various ways trying to put the screws on her.”
Officials in Beijing still want a retraction of the prime minister’s November 2025 comments but it’s unlikely, Kingston believes.
The Japanese government has verbally protested against Chinese military moves, tracked Chinese ships with its own, and scrambled fighter jets.
Tokyo is now considering a 70 trillion to 80 trillion yen (as high as $508 billion) defense spending plan for the five-year period beginning in April 2027, up from 43 trillion yen in the previous half-decade span, Japanese media outlets have reported.
“As the security environment becomes increasingly severe, cooperation with the ally and like-minded countries is indispensable to peace and stability in the region,” Japan’s Ministry of Defense said in an Oct. 29 statement after a meeting with defense officials from Australia, the Philippines and the United States.
The ministry, it said, “will continue to take advantage of various opportunities to further strengthen such cooperation.”

Across three cohorts in Wave Life Sciences’ mid-stage trial of WVE-007, higher baseline body mass index and excessive body fat have been associated with a more pronounced effect, Rodman & Renshaw said following the company’s ObesityWeek update.
Wave Life Sciences is advocating for quality over quantity this holiday season. At ObesityWeek on Sunday, the biotech presented initial data from patients taking a high dose of its weight loss candidate WVE-007, painting an overall picture that analysts say support the hypothesis that baseline body composition is associated with greater therapeutic effects.
“In our view, the data reinforce the baseline-adiposity thesis behind [Wave’s] Phase 2a design,” Rodman & Renshaw analysts wrote in a note to investors on Friday.
Wave’s Phase 1/2a INLIGHT trial is studying WVE-007—an investigational GalNAc-siRNA designed to knock down the activin E protein—in around 400 people with a higher body mass index (BMI), defined by Wave as 35–50 kg/m², and higher baseline adiposity, or excessive body fat. The trial includes patients with and without type 2 diabetes.
Loss-of-function mutations in the INHBE gene encoding activin E have been linked to better body composition. Activin E is considered a potential therapeutic target for abdominal obesity as it promotes fat storage, among other roles.
Body composition has been a challenge with weight loss therapies currently on the market, as experts flag overcoming muscle loss as a key unmet need—particularly in older adults. Companies like Wave and Veru are trying to address this problem.
IN PARTNERSHIP WITH GEMPHARMATECH
Beyond GLP‑1s: The race for next‑gen obesity drugs starts in the preclinical models
Efficacy plateaus, muscle loss and weight rebound are testing the limits of GLP-1 success, pushing companies toward new mechanisms and multitarget designs to close the gap. But progress depends on understanding disease biology and selecting the right drug candidates to derisk clinical trials.
September 2, 2026
·
5 min read
·
Jennifer C. Smith-Parker
Read more
On Sunday, Wave presented six-month data from the highest dose cohort (600 mg) of WVE-007 in the Phase 1 portion of the study. The therapy was “generally safe and well tolerated through 600 mg,” with no patients dropping out of the study, no serious treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and no deaths, according to the company’s abstract , which was posted on Friday. Safety and tolerability are the study’s primary endpoints.
As for efficacy, visceral fat and waist circumference fell versus placebo and lean mass was preserved but total fat was relatively unchanged, Rodman & Renshaw said on Friday. The analysts attributed these results, which they said were similar to the 400 mg cohort, to the lower baseline BMI of these cohorts rather than a dose-response failure.
Across the 240-mg, 400-mg and 600-mg dose levels, “higher baseline BMI and adiposity were associated with a more pronounced effect,” Rodman & Renshaw said on Friday.
Wave also reported dose-dependent reductions in activin E for up to six months across all four dose levels, including the lowest 75-mg dose.
In March, Wave reported that a 240-mg dose of WVE-007 led to placebo-adjusted visceral fat reduction of 14.3%, plus reductions in total fat, waist circumference and body weight of 5.3%, 3.3% and 0.9% after six months. WVE-007 also preserved lean mass, with a 2.4% increase as measured by medical imaging. This cohort has the highest BMI, Rodman & Renshaw noted.
Obesity
Wave Stock Cut in Half on Underwhelming Higher Dose Obesity Data
While participants on a lower dose of Wave Life Sciences’ RNA therapy lost 5.3% total fat at the six-month mark, those receiving the higher dose saw a less than 1% drop at three months.
March 26, 2026
·
2 min read
·
Tristan Manalac
Read more
However, three-month data from the 400-mg dose released at the same time failed to impress analysts, causing Wave to lose more than half of its market share. Participants in this cohort saw 5% visceral fat loss, 0.2% loss of lean mass and total fat loss of less than 1%.
In a note at the time, Leerink Partners said investors were “likely discouraged” by these data, “which look similar on visceral fat as 240 mg and not as good on total fat and lean mass.”
In a note on Sunday, William Blair attributed the 400-mg data to the fact that 10 of 24 patients “already had healthy visceral fat levels, which leaves little fat to lose.”
Next up, Wave expects six-month data from its Phase 2a trial of WVE-007 in patients with high BMI, high adiposity and comorbidities, in 2027. These data will be “critical” to defining the drug’s clinical profile and relevance, William Blair wrote in an October investor note, as this population is more representative of the obesity population.
Also this weekend, Wave held a continuing medical education event where panelists from Wave, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard and health provider knownwell “argued that body composition and broader outcomes drive successful management, given the lifelong dosing and disease burden,” Rodman & Renshaw recapped in a Saturday note to investors. “They want the headline weight-loss number challenged with the quality of that weight loss.”
The firm said these views are aligned with a study recently published in Nature of 844,108 adults, “where fat distribution and organ dysfunction predicted risk better than body mass index.”
Other takeaways from the panel included that, beyond weight loss, comorbidity improvement was physicians’ top preference, ahead of muscle and function and tolerability; as for unmet needs, durability was first, with tolerability and treatment burden second.
“Adipose tissue is central to both the obesity and the comorbidity problem,” Rodman & Renshaw wrote of the panelists’ conclusions.

precursor_events.source_quote: Wave also reported dose-dependent reductions in activin E for up to six months across all four dose levels, including the lowest 75-mg dose.
In a note at the time, Leerink Partners said investors were “likely discouraged” by these data, “which look similar on visceral fat as 240 mg and not as good on total fat and lean mass.”

precursor_events.source_quote: These data will be “critical” to defining the drug’s clinical profile and relevance, William Blair wrote in an October investor note, as this population is more representative of the obesity population.

Also this weekend, Wave held a continuing medical education event where panelists from Wave, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard and health provider knownwell “argued that body composition and broader outcomes drive successful management, given the lifelong dosing and disease burden,” Rodman & Renshaw recapped in a Saturday note to investors.
